utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case before us today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-83-A, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would first like to inquire whether Mr. Delic can follow the proceedings in a language he understands. Thank you, Mr. Delic, for telling us so. Could I please have the appearances, starting with Mr. Delic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all in the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and John Jones for the Defence of General Delic, with Lejla Gluhic and Sabina Dzubur as our assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And on the Prosecution side?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours. Peter Kremer appearing on the Prosecution, assisted by Todd Schneider, Elena Martin-Salgado, Kyle Wood, and our assistant this morning is Lourdes Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kremer. First of all, I recall that a Status Conference was held on the 6th of February, 2009, pursuant to Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Having consulted the parties and on account of the fact that Rasim Delic was on conditional release in the period pending appeal, it was decided not to hold any further appeal Status Conferences. The Appeals Chamber is sitting today to hear the parties' submissions related to the appeals filed by Rasim Delic and the Prosecution against the trial judgement. Before I give the floor to the parties, let me briefly summarise the grounds of appeal pending before the Appeals Chamber and I will also outline the way the hearing the proceed today. In its judgement of 15th of September, 2008, Trial Chamber I made up of Judge Moloto, Presiding Judge, Judges Harhoff and Lattanzi, sentenced by a majority decision Rasim Delic to a single sentence of three years of imprisonment for the count he was found guilty of, namely, Count 2, cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Articles 3 and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal in relation to events in Livade and the Kamenica camp from July to September 1995. Rasim Delic appealed against the trial judgement and the Prosecution appealed against the sentence against Rasim Delic. Under his first ground of appeal, Rasim Delic submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law or in fact in finding that he had effective control over the El Mujahed Detachment from July to December 1995. First, he contends that the Trial Chamber erred in fact in relation to the indicators of effective control that it found to have existed and in failing to consider indicators of lack of effective control. Second, Delic contends that the Trial Chamber failed to draw the proper inferences from its findings and from the evidence regarding the structure, functioning, and role of the ABiH, the RBiH Presidency, the KM Kakanj, and the chain of command within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Third, Delic submits that the Trial Chamber erred when it found that the ABiH organisation improved considerably in the period between 1993 and 1995, allowing Delic to exercise effective control over the EMD. Fourth, Delic contends that the Trial Chamber erred in law in misapplying the burden and the standard of proof. Fifth, Delic argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law by denying him the right to a fair trial when convicting him on the basis of his superior-subordinate relationship to the EMD, whereas it was not pleaded in the indictment. Under his second ground of appeal, Delic contends that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he had reason to know that members of the EMD were about to commit or had committed the crime of cruel treatment against VRS soldiers detained by the EMD. First, he argues that by virtue of the cumulative effect of a number of errors, the Trial Chamber erred in fact, occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Second, the Delic submits that the Trial Chamber erred when it found that he had received information concerning the EMD's record of misdemeanours and criminal offences and that this information was such as to qualify bulletin 137 as sufficiently alarming to justify his immediate intervention in order to determine whether members of the EMD were about to commit or had committed crimes in Livade and the Kamenica camp in July and August 1995 or had committed them. Third, Delic claims that the Trial Chamber erred in law in finding that he had reason to know that crimes had been or were about to be committed on the sole basis that he had sufficiently alarming information at his disposal. Fourth, Delic claims that the Trial Chamber erred both in law and in fact in holding that his failure to conduct an investigation to determine whether EMD members were about to commit or had already committed crimes in Livade and the Kamenica camp in July and August 1995 entailed that he exacted the risk that crimes were about to be committed or had been committed by EMD members in July and August 1995. Fifth, Delic argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law in finding that Delic's alleged knowledge of less serious offences committed by the EMD which did not contain the elements of cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war was sufficient to put him on notice that the more serious offences of cruel treatment would be committed by the EMD. Lastly, in his third and last ground of appeal, Rasim Delic claims that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he had not taken the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent and punish the cruel treatment inflicted by members of the El Mujahed Detachment on soldiers of the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina detained in Livade and in the Kamenica camp in July and August 1995. Firstly, Mr. Delic submits that the Trial Chamber committed a two-fold error of law and fact when it held that he had the material ability to prevent and punish the cruel treatment committed in July and August 1995. Secondly, Mr. Delic alleges that the Trial Chamber committed a two-fold error of law and fact when it failed to specify any of the necessary and reasonable measures he could have taken under the circumstances at the time and that were in his power to prevent and punish the crimes committed by the El Mujahed Detachment. Thirdly, Mr. Delic contends that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that neither he or any other individual under his authority or under his leadership or command had taken the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish the cruel treatment inflicted on the detainees in Livade and in the Kamenica camp in July and August 1995. Fourthly, Mr. Delic submits that the Trial Chamber erred when it relied on the information contained in bulletin 137 to establish his responsibility for failing to prevent or punish the crimes. Mr. Delic, therefore, requests the Appeals Chamber to quash his conviction and to substitute it for a finding of not guilty. The Prosecution objects to Rasim Delic arguments. The Prosecution more specifically claims that the Trial Chamber committed no error of fact or law when it concluded that Mr. Delic exercised effective control over the members of the El Mujahed Detachment, that he had reason to know that members of this detachment were about to commit crimes or that they had committed them, and that Rasim Delic failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish the crimes. As stated above, the Prosecution appeals against Rasim Delic's three-year sentence. The Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber correctly stated the law that applies to sentencing, but that it erred in law in imposing a manifestly inadequate sentence. Firstly, the Prosecution alleges that the Trial Chamber's sentence does not reflect the appallingly brutal nature of the crimes committed by Rasim Delic's subordinates. Secondly, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber did not sufficiently consider the gravity of Rasim Delic's breach of his duties as a commander. Thirdly, the Prosecution claims that the Trial Chamber erred when it failed to consider the likely sentence of Rasim Delic's subordinates. And fourthly, the Prosecution claims that the Trial Chamber failed to meet the two main objectives of sentencing that apply to international crimes, namely, deterrence and retribution. The Prosecution requests the Trial Chamber -- the Appeals Chamber to impose a more appropriate sentence of seven years' imprisonment. At this hearing, the counsel of the parties may submit their grounds and subgrounds of appeal in the order they consider the most appropriate. I would nonetheless like to remind the parties that they have been asked to develop three questions which have been disclosed to them in the addendum to the Scheduling Order of the 15th of December, 2009, questions I shall not go over here. I shall now remind you of the standards that apply to errors of fact and errors of law on appeal. Appeals against trial judgements do not give rise to a trial de novo. The parties may not merely repeat the arguments that the Trial Chamber has heard already. It follows from Article 25 of the Statute that the Appeals Chamber's role is limited to correcting errors of law that invalidate the decision and errors of fact that have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. Consequently, the party alleging an error on a question of law must present arguments in support of its claim and explain how the error invalidates a decision. As for errors of fact, it is well established in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that the Appeals Chamber does not lightly disturb findings of fact reached by a Trial Chamber. The Appeals Chamber will thus only intervene once it has been established that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the same finding or when that finding is wholly erroneous. Moreover, the Appeals Chamber may summarily dismiss, without considering them on their merits, arguments submitted by a party that have no chance of reversing or setting aside the impugned decision. The appealing parties must also provide specific references of the material presented in support of their arguments on appeal. In addition, the Appeals Chamber must not be expected to analyse the findings of the parties in detail if they are obscure, contradictory, or vague, or if they suffer from other formal and obvious insufficiencies. Lastly, the Appeals Chamber has an inherent power to determine which arguments merit a reasoned response in writing and which arguments may be dismissed without any detailed reasoning because they are evidently unfounded. This hearing will proceed according to the addendum to the Scheduling Order of December -- of 15th of December, 2009. The Defence will start submitting its arguments this morning for one hour and a quarter. After a 30-minute break, the Prosecutor may submit its arguments in response for 50 minutes. After the Prosecution's response, the Defence will have 20 minutes to submit its arguments in reply. After one -- a one-hour lunch break, the Prosecution may submit its arguments for one hour. The Defence will have 50 minutes to submit its arguments in response. The Prosecution will then have 20 minutes to submit its arguments in reply. Finally, Mr. Delic will be invited to take the floor, if he wishes to, for a short statement lasting no longer than ten minutes. Arguments presented clearly, logically, and concisely would greatly assist the Appeals Chamber. The Judges will take the liberty to interrupt the parties at any time to ask for clarifications or to put questions. This is what I wish to share with you. If there are no questions on the conduct of these proceedings, I would now like to invite the Defence to submit its arguments on appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm obliged. By way of preliminary, we've prepared bundles containing extracts of the case law to which I'll refer in the course of answering the first of the Chamber's questions. So I wonder if we could distribute that now. There are six copies, one for the Prosecutor and five for the Bench and one for the Registry. And, Your Honours, looking at the clock, I see that it's nearly 10.00. I take it, then, that I can go until 11.15. I realise that's slightly later than the Scheduling Order --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged. Your Honours, this morning I'm going to address the three questions posed by the Chamber, but I'd like to start, if I may, by encapsulating our appeal on ground one in one core submission, which is this. The conclusion of Judge Harhoff and Judge Lattanzi on effective control simply does not follow from their own findings. Against the backdrop of the Chamber's own findings on effective control, their conclusion is a non sequitur. That's their error. A reasonable trier of fact doesn't reach conclusions which are contradicted by their own findings, and that's also why Judge Moloto's dissent is so important, because his conclusion does follow from the Chamber's findings. Excuse me, I'm obliged to my colleague. As a matter of law, logic, and fact, Judge Moloto's conclusion does follow and his dissent shows that the only reasonable view of the case was that there was at least a reasonable doubt that Delic exercised effective control over the EMD. And so the majority erred and they occasioned a miscarriage of justice. Fortuitously, Your Honours' first question helps me to illustrate that point, and so I turn to the indicators of effective control. We say the case law establishes at least the following 12 propositions. The first proposition. In order to establish effective control it must be shown not only that an accused issued orders, but that those orders were in fact obeyed by the perpetrators. This proposition is well established and finds expression, for example, in the Strugar appeal judgement at paragraph 256, whether a superior's orders are, in fact, followed can be indicative of a superior's effective control over the subordinates. The Appeals Chamber notes that in addition to finding that Strugar had the authority to issue orders, the Trial Chamber also established that Strugar's orders were actually followed. And we rely for that proposition too on the Halilovic appeal judgement, paragraph 207; the Hadzihasanovic appeal judgement, paragraph 199; and the Dragomir Milosevic appeal judgement, at paragraph 280. It follows that a counter-indicator of effective control is disregard or noncompliance by the perpetrators with orders or instructions issued by the accused. This is usefully illustrated by the Hadzihasanovic appeal judgement at paragraphs 225 to 227, where the Appeals Chamber dealt with the ABiH 3rd Corps' inability to obtain the release of one of its own soldiers who had been abducted, detained, and mistreated by the EMD for consuming alcohol. Although the 3rd Corps commander ordered his release, the EMD did not obey, nor did they release him even when threatened with attack. As the Appeals Chamber noted at paragraph 227: "The EMD was never requested by the 3rd Corps to catch hostages, nor did it receive any approval for doing so. Quite to the contrary, its behaviour was in reckless disregard of the 3rd Corps' requests that it abstain from these abductions. It did not comply with Mehmed Alagic's order to release them or release them when threatened with the use of force." And so the Appeals Chamber found that: "These events confirm that Hadzihasanovic did not have effective control over the El Mujahed Detachment and: "Demonstrate that there were areas in which the EMD acted independently from the 3rd Corps." Paragraph 226. These facts are, of course, strikingly similar to the facts of this case. Indeed, we say, the evidence is much stronger, as you'll see from paragraphs 403 to 404 of the judgement, where the Chamber held that by capturing and holding VRS soldiers who were mistreated, in July and August 1995, the very events for which Delic was convicted: "The EMD did not comply with the obligations as set out by the 35th Division commander concerning the handling of captives taken during combat," and that the EMD acted "in defiance of ABiH orders, in defiance of ABiH orders." Yet Judges Harhoff and Lattanzi failed to draw the obvious conclusion from this, the conclusion reached by the Appeals Chamber in Hadzihasanovic and by Judge Moloto in this case, in particular at paragraph 27 of his dissent, namely, that such events showed that the accused did not have effective control over the EMD. And a litany of orders disobeyed by the EMD is further set out by the Chamber at paragraphs 371 to 385 of the judgement. The second proposition, evidence that the alleged subordinates reserved their right to participate or not to participate in combat is a counter-indicator of effective control. The Hadzihasanovic trial judgement provides authority for that proposition. At paragraph 795, the Chamber referred to evidence: "That the Mujahedin reserved the right to decide for themselves whether or not to join combat." In this case too, the Chamber clearly found that the EMD "made their own decisions" about whether to participate in combat, paragraph 382, and that the EMD would simply "decline to take part in a given ABiH operation" if they deemed the conditions not met. In other words, the EMD simply made up their own mind whether to participate in combat, regardless of what the ABiH ordered. If that's effective control, then it has to be said it's not very effective. The third proposition, erratic behaviour and prior instances of indiscipline on the part of the alleged subordinates is relevant to assessing effective control. This proposition is found, for example, in the Strugar appeal judgement at paragraph 257, where the Appeals Chamber found that: "Evidence of prior instances of indiscipline and of noncompliance with orders would be clearly relevant to an assessment of whether Strugar had effective control over his subordinates." Likewise, in the Oric appeal judgement: "The Appeals Chamber considers that if a superior-subordinate relationship existed, it cannot be relevant to ask whether the subordinate's behaviour was erratic. However, if it is not clear whether that relationship existed, it can be relevant to take into account the erratic behaviour of the subordinate in determining whether the superior had the 'material ability to prevent or punish' necessary for effective control." Paragraph 159. That observation is clearly relevant here. In this case it was, at the very least, not clear that a superior-subordinate relationship existed between Delic and the EMD. Indeed, we say, it was abundantly clear that the EMD members were not Delic's subordinates. So in those circumstances it was highly relevant to take into account the erratic behaviour of EMD members in determining whether Delic had effective control. The majority entirely failed to do so. There was a super-abundance of evidence of the EMD's erratic and dangerous behaviour, by which I mean dangerous to the ABiH whom EMD members habitually threatened and abused. See paragraph 408 of the judgement. So one is in a sense spoiled for choice. In E 774, for example, one finds this account of a dispute between the EMD and a regular ABiH unit: "On this occasion," and this is July 1995, precise time of these -- the events at which Delic was convicted. "On this occasion, members of the El Mujahed were saying that the basic objective of their struggle was to exterminate the Serbs and Croats and added that they were expecting from everyone to remain on the path of Allah, and sooner or later the two units, i.e., the EMD and the ABiH unit in question, would clash because of their difference." And one sees the same thing in dozens of exhibits, E 125, E 667, E 670, E 760 -- sorry, E 737, E 800, E 801, E 872, E 892, E 903, E 934, E 938, E 1084, each of which I would urge the Appeals Chamber to review in order to get a true flavour of how the EMD behaved, how dangerous to other ABiH units, and how wild and completely ungovernable they were. And Prosecution witnesses, Hasanagic, Imamovic, Sljuka, and Sehic, all told the same story at T3102, T4058, T4370, and T5086, respectively. And really, there can be no dispute as to the bizarre erratic, and dangerous behaviour of the EMD. The fourth proposition, effective control is absent when the perpetrators have the independent power to take decisions and to act. Thus, in the Oric trial judgement at paragraph 706, the Chamber found that local armed groups "were primarily loyal to their respective commanders" and acted independently. And, therefore, it followed they were not under Oric's effective control. Again, we say this applies a fortiori to the EMD and Delic's command. "The EMD had a 'religious council,' the shura, which was its supreme decision-making body." Those are the Chamber's own words, its own finding at paragraph 189 of the judgement. And "the shura was the final authority, the final authority, within the EMD regarding all matters of importance. The Emir was elected by and answerable to the shura; his decisions could be amended or overturned only by that body." Again, the Chamber's own words from the same paragraph, and it was to the Emir alone that the EMD were loyal. In our submission, the fact, as found by the Chamber, that the supreme decision-making body, the final authority over the EMD was not the ABiH, but the religious council, the shura, cannot be reconciled with there not even being a reasonable doubt as to effective control. Look what Ismet Alija, again a Prosecution witness, said about the EMD. "In my knowledge and according to my information, the EMD was not within the system of command and control. They were a closed unit and they stood for themselves. They were independent. They were very difficult to reach or receive information about their activities. They made their own decisions." He went on to explain the shura: "Your Honours, I believe that you know that they had their own way of decision-making. That term is 'shura,' is something like a council of sorts. And if they decided to do something, they did it. And if they decided not to do, they didn't do it. And they would not take anybody's orders." T4156. Those are the words of a Prosecution witness. How striking is that? As with all Prosecution witnesses, I emphasise the fact because, in our submission, the Prosecution cannot credibly go behind or seek to contradict the words of its own witnesses, not if they haven't had them declared hostile. The fifth proposition is that an insufficiently developed or dysfunctional chain of command is a counter-indicator of effective control. That proposition is axiomatic and finds expression, inter alia, in the Oric trial judgement at paragraph 707. The sixth proposition is that evidence that the alleged subordinates did not regard themselves as being under the command of the alleged superior and vice versa indicates a lack of effective control. Authority for that proposition is to be found, inter alia, in the Hadzihasanovic trial judgement at paragraph 795, where the Chamber referred to the evidence that: "3rd Corps commanders did not believe they had the authority to give orders to the Mujahedin." In this case, again on the Chamber's own finding, the EMD stated: "'We are now one unit, we have our own body which is formally under the control of the [ABiH], but the [ABiH] cannot order us to engage in actions against our will.'" I hope to revert to the matter later if I have time, but the very concept that one cannot be ordered to engage in actions against one's will gives the line to the idea that there is compliance when the EMD went along with all this. They're not following orders or obeying orders if it simply coincides with what you would do anyway. That's the Chamber's finding at paragraph 381, and we would also refer you to its findings at paragraphs 432 and 453 in that regard. And this was also the evidence of Prosecution Witness Imamovic, T4045; Prosecution Witness Sljuka, T4301, and T4369; Prosecution Witness Hajderhodzic at T3784; Prosecution Witness Husic at T446; and Prosecution Witness Awad at T172 of the Sarajevo hearing. Time and again, former EMD members in this trial gave evidence that they did not consider themselves a part of the ABiH at all and exhibits bore that out. Yet, the majority didn't consider this aspect at all as detracting from or creating a reasonable doubt as to effective control. The seventh proposition concerns reporting, evidence that the perpetrators did not submit reports to the alleged superior and/or that they did submit reports to other superiors is a counter-indicator of effective control. We refer to the Hadzihasanovic trial judgement at paragraph 795, which refers to the relevance of the fact that there was "no evidence indicating that the Mujahedin sent combat reports or other reports on their activities to those in charge of the combat in which they took part." Now, reporting is key to effective control. As Judge Moloto correctly pointed out in his dissent at paragraph 15: "The EMD's failure to report to its immediately superior unit coupled with the EMD's erratic behaviour towards the orders of the ABiH seriously undermined the command and control of Rasim Delic. A chain of command lies in the flow of orders and information, the transmission of information up and down the chain of command, and the ability of a commander to exercise his authority through orders constitute the two essential components of a system of command and control. Only if these two components function is a commander in a position to control his units and induce obedience from them. However, this did not happen in relation to the EMD." Yet again, the majority's conclusion regarding effective control is belied by its own findings. The Chamber found or at least did not dispute that "the EMD never submitted written or oral operative reports to the 35th Division," its allegedly superior unit in the ABiH, paragraph 424 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Yes, Judge Meron, has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 430 of the judgement, last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't catch the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry, paragraph 430 of the judgement. "Although the EMD was officially re-subordinated to the 35th Division ... it orally reported several times to the 3rd Corps command on the progress of the combat activities," how to reconcile this with your argument, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And the fact that there is some evidence of oral reporting by the EMD to its superior's commanders, would this not indicate a level of control?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, the position with the 3rd Corps and the 35th Division in itself is extremely revealing about the lack of effective control, because according to the evidence as accepted by the Chamber, the principle of unity of command meant that subordinate units reported to their next superior unit, which was the 35th Division. So already the fact that the EMD simply disregarded that and when they felt like it went over the heads of the 35th Division to the 3rd Corps, reveals that they didn't care [indiscernible] about the system which was meant to be in place. As to oral reporting, we would respectfully adopt what Judge Moloto says in relation to that, which is that oral reporting, firstly when written reports are required to be submitted, hardly meets the requirements imposed within the ABiH. But oral reporting, the evidence showed, was entirely consistent with two allied units fighting together, ensuring before an action that they didn't end up shooting each other. It's something which any allied co-operative fighting unit would do in order to avoid friendly fire. It's common sense. The majority suggested that this was because there was a language problem, which we've dealt with in our appeals brief. It's a non-explanation. Because of the Bosnian speakers in the EMD, they could have easily submitted written reports if they wanted to. The fact that the majority felt that they needed to make that explanation is itself revealing. I don't know if that assists. Now, by contrast, the EMD did send detailed written reports to its foreign masters. See, for example -- sorry, is there another question from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Judge Liu had a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I wonder whether you finished your answer. If not, you may continue; and after that I'll raise my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I am finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Well, I believe that in your presentations you mentioned the insufficiently developed and dysfunctional chain of command in the ABiH and EMD, and you also mentioned the case law in Hadzihasanovic's case. I understand, you know, that the Appeals Chamber overturned the Trial Chamber's finding of effective control in that case. But I wonder whether you noticed the time difference between the Hadzihasanovic case and the present case. I believe the crimes of which Mr. Hadzihasanovic was convicted was committed between January and September 1993, while in the present case which took place in July and August 1995. The Trial Chamber specifically found out that the command and control improved significantly from 1993 to 1995. Therefore, the circumstances of the present case are materially different from those of the Hadzihasanovic case. What's your comments on this time difference? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If I didn't make it clear, I apologise. We rely on Hadzihasanovic appeal judgement purely for the legal principles. That's what I was extracting, and it would be clearly simplistic in the extreme to say, well, there was an acquittal on appeal in Hadzihasanovic and we're entitled to the same acquittal. Obviously, there's a two-year difference. However, the majority's conclusion, that's at paragraph 460: "The Majority finds that the structure, organisation as well as command and control within the ABiH improved significantly from the time when Delic was appointed as Commander" in 1993 until 1995. That's the premise of the majority which distinguishes, if you like, Hadzihasanovic. But if you look at that paragraph there is no reference to any evidence at all. It's pure assertion, and we've dealt in detail in our appeals brief and why we say that's not based on evidence. It's contradicted by the evidence. It's very revealing, they don't cite any evidence there. Surely that's a moment to cite to a witness who says, well, things improved a lot in those two years. No one said that. The exhibits didn't show it. That was their own way to get around Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In relation to reporting the other component is the EMD did send - and this is revealing - detailed written reports to its foreign masters. And I was referring to, as you'll see, a very detailed combat report at paragraph 444 of the judgement. If you have it out, I'll ask you to turn it up because it's revealing. The report is so specific it refers to how the assault groups began to advance at 12.02 a.m. It gives the exact geographical differences between the different areas involved in the combat. Nothing like that was sent to the alleged superiors in the ABiH, but it was sent abroad. And in terms of oral communication, I've touched on this but I'll perhaps reiterate it, it's hardly surprising that there was some oral communication between the EMD and ABiH units before or during combat because it would be suicide not to, just as it would be suicide for the EMD to launch its own combat operations without telling anyone else. And the majority seemed to consider it significant that the EMD didn't just launch attacks without telling anyone, but obviously, obviously, they wouldn't, if not -- if only for their own self-preservation. And that's what allies do: They communicate in order to co-ordinate their respective combat activities. The French and British forces did it at the Battle of the Marne in the First World War. Allies do it today to avoid friendly fire. It's obvious. And this highlights a crucial point about the flaws in the majority's reasoning. If oral reporting is consistent with nothing more than co-operation, then oral reporting doesn't prove effective control. Indeed, in relation to each indicator, we invite the Appeals Chamber to ask the Prosecution this question: What did the Trial Chamber find which is consistent only with effective control, not consistent with anything else? And the answer is: Nothing. Or putting the question the other way: Is there any finding by the Chamber which is wholly inconsistent with co-ordination, co-operation, joint or mutual assistance or even attempts to establish control, all of which would fall short of effective control? And again the answer will inevitably be: No, there is nothing. The majority should have been able to say: We rule out that these are just two armies co-operating with each other, because if it were only that and not effective control, then X, Y, and Z, but you won't find that in the judgement. They never did that. Which means that Delic had to be acquitted and that his conviction should be quashed now. I turn to the eighth proposition, which is that where authority exists over the perpetrators from persons other than the accused, then that indicates absence of effective control. We refer to paragraphs 216 and 217 of the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura appeal judgement, from which two points of principle emerge. First, that: "Effective control cannot be established by process of elimination." So we didn't have to show that someone else had effective control over the EMD, but for the Trial Chamber could conclude that Delic did not. Second, that if authority was exercised over the perpetrators by persons other than the accused, then that is a relevant counter-indicator of effective control. That's obvious. No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will hold to the one and despise the other. That's the parable of the unjust steward. In this case there was abundant evidence accepted by the Chamber that authority over the EMD was exerted by foreign state organs, Islamic organisations such as the ICI, and high-ranking Muslim clerics. The ninth proposition is that a key indicator of effective control is whether the perpetrators received weapons and ammunition from the accused. This indicator is clearly expressed in the report of the International Commission of Inquiry on Darfur of 25 January 2005, at paragraphs 111 and 113. The Appeals Chamber will appreciate the chairman of that commission was Antonio Cassese - the first President of this Tribunal and now President of the Special Tribunal for Lebanon - and so while the report is not case law as such, we say it is of strong persuasive authority. In finding "clear links between the Sudanese state and militias, the commission relied as an indicator of effective control, the fact that militias received weapons and regular supplies of ammunition from the army and other state organs." In this case, the Chamber found that the ABiH's assistance to the EMD in terms of ammunition and weaponry was "sporadic and insufficient." Paragraph 418. Conversely, there was abundant evidence that the EMD obtained arms and munition and ammunition from their own sources. Prosecution's own witness Awad, a former EMD member, testified: "We had our own independent logistics and we were stronger than the corps as far as that is concerned." That's T260 on 10.2.08. And the Chamber referred to this unchallenged evidence in footnote 1079 of the judgement and apparently accepted it. This was also borne out by PW-9's evidence at T5682 and by E 676. The tenth proposition may be captured by the dictum, he who pays the piper calls the tune; or in other words, control of the finances and salaries paid to the perpetrators is another indicator of effective control. But for this proposition again we cite the Darfur report, paragraph 113, referring to the payment of monthly salaries as an indicator of control. And the Musema trial judgement at paragraph 880 where the Trial Chamber found that Musema had effective control over the employees of the Gisovu Tea Factory, inter alia, because "he exercised legal and financial control over these employees." In this case, the Chamber found that "the EMD was financed through separate channels," separate from the ABiH. And that the salaries of EMD members "came from funds secured by the EMD." That's paragraphs 418 to 419 of the judgement. The evidence in terms of the EMD's financing was incontrovertible. We refer to E 782, the evidence of Prosecution witness PW-9 at T8633 and E 1201, from which you can see the ICI, the Islamic Cultural Institute, sent monthly payments to the EMD. The Chamber accepted this exhibit at footnote 1145. The point about salaries was picked up by Judge Moloto at paragraph 18 of his dissent: "The links of the EMD with the foreign authorities show another area in which the EMD acted independently from the ABiH. Indeed, none of the EMD members was paid by the ABiH." That's a very striking fact. I continue. "Furthermore, the fact that these contacts were put in place by the EMD with a view to promoting its cause and attract funds may also allow the inference that the authorities sponsoring the EMD might have retained a significant influence over them." And as an aside here, I would make an important point that Judge Moloto and the majority shared the same factual findings; they simply drew different conclusions from them. It's an obvious inference and an obvious point but one which escaped the majority. He who holds the purse strings is clearly in a position to dictate terms, to exercise control, and precisely by the threat of cutting off financial support if his orders are not followed. The ABiH and Delic crucially were never in a position to make that threat, to exert control through holding the purse strings. They couldn't threaten to stop paying the EMD if the EMD didn't obey orders because they weren't paying [Realtime transcript read in error "saying"] them. It's as simply as that. And -- sorry, correction in the transcript because they weren't paying them. Indeed one finds that obvious logic that money equals control or the potential for control reflected in the Tribunal's jurisprudence from the earliest days in the Tadic appeal judgement of 15th July 1999 in the context of deciding whether the VRS was under the control of the FRY government. One of the decisive factors for the Appeals Chamber was "'the continuing payment of salaries, to Bosnian Serb and non-Bosnian Serb officers alike, by the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.'" That's paragraph 150. The 11th proposition is to prove effective control it must be shown that the accused has disciplinary and investigative powers over the perpetrators as a result of his position of authority, that those powers were actual and effective as opposed to merely formal and unenforceable, and finally that those measures were capable of punishing the crimes that were the basis of the charges and not some other crimes. For example, ordinary crimes like theft. Whereas here it's alleged that the accused had effective control on the basis that crimes by the perpetrators, the EMD, were on occasion punished. There are two separate questions which have to be asked: Who initiated the prosecution and was the prosecution for war crimes or for ordinary crimes? The issue is addressed, for example, in the Oric appeal judgement at paragraph 142, where the Chamber held that Oric's alleged ability to take disciplinary action against the perpetrators was not demonstrated by the fact that he had been "'... instrumental in promoting an investigation'" of the military police chief. Since the Trial Chamber "did not find that Oric took this measure, or was able to do so, as a result of an authority on his part over the military police." The Appeals Chamber therefore quashed Oric's conviction, ruling that the Trial Chamber had erred in finding that Oric exercised effective control over the military police. When we turn back to this case, two very striking facts emerge from the Chamber's findings. One, there was no evidence that Delic was able to discipline EMD members at all. In the section of the judgement dealing with the ability to investigate and punish EMD members, the Chamber was only able to point to criminal proceedings brought against foreign members of the EMD for "illegal behaviour although not for violations of international humanitarian law." Paragraph 470. That's a crucial fact of which the majority failed entirely to appreciate the significance. Second, the criminal proceedings relied on by the majority were not brought by Delic or even by the military, but by the civilian authorities. So in this way the majority fell into the exact same error as the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber. In Hadzihasanovic, the Trial Chamber relied on the domestic prosecution of an EMD member to show Hadzihasanovic's authority to punish EMD members. And the Appeals Chamber found that this was an error. At paragraph 219 of the Hadzihasanovic appeal judgement it's stated: "Witness Siljak testified that the alleged perpetrator 'had to appear before the court in Travnik' without specifying which court it was. Even if it were true that the said individual had been brought before the Travnik district military court, there is no indication in the trial judgement as to what role Hadzihasanovic would have had in bringing about the initiation of proceedings against that perpetrator. Nor does Witness Siljak's testimony demonstrate that the perpetrator was prosecuted following measures taken or initiated by the 3rd Corps. The Appeals Chamber stresses that the perpetrator was an identified local Muslim and that both the civilian police and the witness himself may have filed the complaint against him." The exact same situation applies to the Trial Chamber's findings in this case. The majority relied on the arrest of EMD members for the killing of the British aid worker, Paul Goodall, referred to at paragraph 448 of the judgement. Yet, those proceedings were instituted by the Ministry of Interior, civilian ministry, before a civilian court, as the Chamber itself accepted. And that's clear too from Exhibit 887, which is referred to in footnote 1158 of the judgement. The Ministry of Interior civilian police brought a criminal report to the civilian prosecutor in Zenica against the EMD. That has nothing to do with the military or Delic. Likewise, with Exhibit 880 relied on by the majority, see footnote 1164, these were criminal proceedings for theft, an ordinary crime, not one of international humanitarian law. And as in Hadzihasanovic, the perpetrator was an identified local Bosnian Muslim, Sefik Bijelo. And in none of this was there any evidence as to what role Delic would have had in bringing about the initiation of proceedings against the perpetrator. So we say that the Appeals Chamber's reasoning for overruling the Trial Chamber in Hadzihasanovic applies equally here, and the Chamber's findings, we say, at paragraphs 447 to 453 of the judgement are, therefore, absolutely incapable as a matter of law of supporting the majority's conclusion at paragraph 470 that Delic had the material ability to investigate, prevent, and punish war crimes committed by the EMD in July/August 1995. I turn to our 12th and final proposition, which is that effective control is absent if the alleged superior needs to negotiate or have recourse to external pressure to ensure compliance with his decisions and orders. Here, too, we rely on the Hadzihasanovic appeal judgement at paragraph 227, which is worth citing in full. "The independence of the El Mujahedin Detachment from the 3rd Corps, as opposed to its subordination to it, is further confirmed by other circumstances. The 3rd Corps had to engage in negotiations for the release of the hostages with some members of the detachment while at the same time putting pressure on them with the support of certain international organisations, as well as Muslim clerics and naturalised Bosnian Muslims. Had the members of the El Mujahedin Detachment been subordinated to the 3rd Corps, no negotiations or external pressure would be necessary -- sorry, would have been needed. The 3rd Corps's orders to release the hostages would have been complied with. Another circumstance showing the independence of the El Mujahedin Detachment from the 3rd Corps is the Trial Chamber's finding that the only means available to the 3rd Corps to obtain the release of the hostages was to use direct force against the El Mujahedin Detachment." And again, we rely on this for legal principle, obviously not for factual finding. It stands to reason that if you can only exercise "control" over a detachment by calling in some outside body, say to someone else, Can you please control these people because we can't, then you yourself are not in control. And that was clearly found to be the case here, as, for example, when the 35th Division commander had to ask municipal authorities for help in dealing with disorderly conduct by EMD members. That's at paragraph 441 in the evidence at footnote 1144 of the judgement. It's as if the head of the British army has to call in the Scotland Yard or the civilian police to deal with the Scots Guards. It's an absurd situation but one which indicates clearly that there was no effective control within the ABiH. And what's even more clear is that if you can only exercise control by attacking and overwhelming the perpetrators, then you're obviously not in control. I mean, otherwise an army which can defeat its enemy in battle would retrospectively be said to have had effective control over the enemy. It's an absurdity. Which calls to mind paragraph 230 of the Hadzihasanovic appeal judgement, where the Chamber said of the relationship between the EMD and 3rd Corps: "It was quite close to overt hostility, since the only way to control the EMD was to attack them as if they were a distinct enemy force." That's quite aside from the impracticality of requiring the ABiH to wage war against the EMD while at the same time fighting the Serbs and the Croats. And the law cannot seriously require Delic to open up a war on, in fact, four fronts, VRS, HVO, Fikret Abdic's forces in Bihac, and the EMD, even if such a decision were up to him, a political decision, which it wasn't. Yet, the evidence shows that's all he could have done to try to bring the EMD fighters under control. And the Chamber's own findings show that's all he could have done. The way that Judges Lattanzi and Harhoff dealt with this is utterly devoid of evidential support or, with the greatest respect to them, common sense. At paragraph 468 they say: "Several witnesses testified that, in their view, nothing could be done to discipline the EMD since coercive measures would have entailed a violent conflict with the EM D." I pause there. That's the evidence. That's the evidence which witnesses have given. Nothing could be done. But then they simply go on to say: "This position is not borne out by facts adduced in the evidence." One would expect, though, wouldn't one, to see what the facts are, a reference, a footnote. What facts? There is nothing, there is nothing there. On such a crucial issue, they simply failed to say what these critically important facts are. No footnote to the evidence, no facts cited, just bald assertion. And then follows one of the most critical passages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. We don't hear the interpretation in French anymore. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There follows one of the most critical passages in their conclusion: "Rather than saying that nothing could be done to oppose undisciplined behaviour of the EMD members, the majority finds that nothing was done or even attempted to be done, in particular in connection with the alleged violations of international humanitarian law during the detention of enemy soldiers and civilians by the EMD. In the majority's view, this failure to take any steps to assume control over the detainees constitutes a failure to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent and punish the crimes in question." Now, there are at least three things fundamentally wrong with this critical conclusion. First, conclusions have to be based on the evidence, and yet the majority here simply rejects out of hand a reasonable view of the evidence, namely, that nothing could be done to control the EMD short of violent conflict, the view taken by the Appeals Chamber in Hadzihasanovic, and the view taken by Judge Moloto in this case, rejected out of hand merely on the basis that that's their preferred view of the matter. Second, the only supporting reasoning provided in footnote 1200, which appears to criticise ABiH officers for not trying again or trying harder when the EMD denied them access to Serb detainees, has got nothing to do with whether Delic had effective control over the EMD. It's one of those non sequiturs. It begs the very question issue, namely, whether if they had tried any harder, it would have made any difference. If the fact is that even if the ABiH officers had tried again or tried harder, it still would have been impossible to gain access to the detainees. Then effective control is absent. The majority leaves that possibility open. In any event, the officers reported the matter, and within four weeks, the detainees were no longer held by the EMD. So the reproach that they should have done more may ring hollow. Thirdly and most fundamentally, the majority in this passage fundamentally confuses the third element of command responsibility. They're discussing effective control here, the first element, and suddenly they skip to the failure to take reasonable measures. "In the majority's view, this failure to take any steps to assume control over the detainees constitutes a failure to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent and punish the crimes." So, in fact, their conclusion doesn't even have anything to do with effective control. So we respectfully submit that the conclusion of Judge Harhoff and Judge Lattanzi is fundamentally confused, flawed, and indefensible. Finally, with regard to question one, we would draw attention to the Appeals Chamber's holding that "criminal responsibility does not attach to a military official merely on the basis of his overall command," paragraph 214, Halilovic appeal judgement, an important and pertinent principle here. I turn to the Chamber's second question, question 2A, whether the Trial Chamber erred by failing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to remind you that you have approximately ten minutes left to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have an hour and 15 minutes, I believe, and I started at 10.00, so I think I have until 11.15, which would be 20 minutes. I will stand corrected if that's wrong. Question 2A, whether the Trial Chamber erred by failing to consider one or more of the indicators of effective control discussed in the trial judgement to be incompatible with the notion of effective control. In our submission, the indicator identified at paragraph 368, VI ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I appreciate there may have been a need to take a break for the tapes or the interpreters. I'll continue until told to stop. The indicator which is identified at paragraph 368, VI, and discussed at paragraphs 416 to 422 of the judgement, mutual assistance between the ABiH and the EMD, is incompatible with the notion of effective control. Assistance, co-operation, or even co-ordination which exists between allied armed forces is plainly not the same thing at all as effective control, and that's -- that runs as a thread through all of the Tribunal's case law. For example, the Hadzihasanovic appeals judgement, paragraph 214: "Thus while these Trial Chamber's findings indicate that the 3rd Corps co-operated with the El Mujahedin Detachment, they are insufficient to establish the existence of effective control." And indeed the Chamber in this case itself had clearly contemplated that forces can fight together without one being under the control of the other. See paragraph 345: "It is not implausible that engagement in combat can take place on the basis of mutual consultations and agreement between two fighting forces as opposed to orders issued from one to the other." And also paragraph 350 that said that the relationship between the Mujahedin as opposed to the EMD and the ABiH "is appropriately characterised as co-operation between such groups as separate and independent military entities rather than subordination of the Mujahedin within the single military structure." On that basis, Delic was found not guilty of the crimes committed in Maline and Bikose in June 1993. But the majority should have applied this same principle to the relationship between the ABiH and the EMD in 1995, but it failed to do so. Its findings are full of the language of consultation, consensus, co-operation, one sees references to requests being addressed from the ABiH to the EMD, requesting authorisation to speak with the commander or to access the camp, not command. For example, the 3rd Corps commander only made "recommendations to the EMD," at paragraph 395 of the judgement, not issuing orders. The 35th Division security officer sought the "approval of the EMD to interview soldiers." A superior doesn't request approval of subordinate units in a matter like this, paragraph 408. The indicator relationship between the EMD and authorities outside the ABiH, depending on how that's construed, is also incompatible with the notion of effective control. The majority's treatment of this issue was superficial in the extreme. At paragraph 464 it stated: "It is true that the EMD communicated with foreign institutions outside Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, in the majority's view, the main purpose of these communications was to promote its cause and attract financial support. Thus, this did not affect the chain of command and the effective control exercised by Rasim Delic over the EMD and its members." The word "thus" in that sentence is singularly misplaced. The conclusion does not follow from the premise. That is again a non sequitur. The EMD communicated with foreign bodies to get finance, the majority finds, it was paid by those bodies, the majority finds, ergo, according to the majority, this had no impact on Delic's effective control. That makes absolutely no sense. It's a classic example of how the majority's conclusions have little or nothing to do with their factual findings. I turn finally to the Appeals Chamber's third question, in essence, whether the Chamber erred in finding that Delic had effective control over the EMD in July and December 1995. Of course, we say they did err. That's the main thrust of our first ground of appeal, so obviously I won't repeat our submissions here. What I may usefully do in the remaining time is simply to outline some major conceptual problems in relation to the majority's findings and conclusions, and the first relates to the very concept of following orders. In relation to the power to give orders and have them executed, just as a preface, I would remind the Chamber of the following findings made by the Chamber, and all paragraph references are to the judgement. The EMD and its members did not reliably execute all of the orders issued by the ABiH, paragraph 371. The EMD refused to surrender a captured tank in August 1995, para 372. The EMD refused an ABiH order to establish a list of all their members; they didn't know who was a member of EMD. They refused an ABiH order to make statements that they had joined army units voluntarily, para 373. And that's crucial because without such a statement they couldn't join the ABiH at all under its rules, you'll see that in paragraph 113 of the judgement. They refused to comply with the decree of the ABiH Ministry of Defence to register with municipal defence secretaries, para 373. They set up the Kamenica camp where they chose to rather than where they had been ordered to, para 374. The commander of the 35th Division could not even threaten the EMD, much less issue orders to them, when they disobeyed orders he could only "invite" their leaders to a meeting, where they would typically just say "God willing, everything is going to be okay," para 375. In combat, as we've seen repeatedly, the EMD themselves said and the Chamber did not dispute: "The ABiH cannot order us to engage in actions against our will," para 381. The EMD would routinely decline to "obey ABiH orders to participate in battle," para 383. And as a former member of the EMD and a Prosecution witness accepted as a fair summary, the ABiH commander would "give orders but unlike other units, you did not accept those orders, you simply decided on your own whether you would accept an order or not," para 384, they accepted that. Even if the EMD did agree to participate in combat, once in the field the EMD commanders would "make their own decisions," para 382. In that situation, the 35th Division commander would not even have influence, not even influence over the EMD much less be in a position to exercise effective control over them. And as we've seen the EMD supreme decision-making body was not the ABiH commander but a shura, para 385. In fact, the EMD's disobedience to orders would be comic if it were not tragic, considering. For example, their plainly absurd excuse, as found by the Chamber, of not going into battle on one occasion because "leaves were falling," which seems to be some sort of joke, and conducting instead a fake attack, a fake attack, the object of which was plainly to deceive the ABiH. And this not surprisingly caused "great distrust of the EMD in the ABiH," paragraphs 389 and 443. They abandoned the positions of the front line without prior notice and for unknown reasons, that's at para 392. And indeed, such was the ABiH's distrust of the EMD that it could not even trust the unit not to "slaughter its own non-Muslim soldiers." You'll see that at paragraph 434 of the judgement. The Chamber found "out of concern for their safety, i.e., the safety of Croatian and Serb ABiH soldiers, battalion command stopped sending its non-Muslim soldiers to the front line. So how on earth, one might ask, is it compatible with the ABiH having effective control over the EMD that the only way they could stop the EMD from slaughtering their own soldiers was by not transferring those soldiers to the front line where they were needed. Notwithstanding this, the majority concluded "the reticent approach," that's their wording, very strange wording. "The reticent approach by the EMD in respect of some superior orders does not create a reasonable doubt as to the general ability of ABiH commanders to have their orders implemented," para 462. And I say "reticent" is a very strange word to use here, it means not saying very much, when what we're talking about is outright defiance and disobedience to orders by the EMD. But underlying this misuse of language, which in itself is revealing, there lies a far more fundamental conceptual mistake, and I'll end on that. I see I have seven minutes left according to my calculation. It's plain that subordinate units which are under effective control are not permitted simply to opt out of war from combat operations as leaves are falling or for whatever other pretext, whatever their reservations about the action. That's simply inconsistent with military reality. And conceptually, an order which you either obey or choose not to obey, depending on your preference or your whim, is not properly understood an order at all. So when the Prosecution says, well, they obeyed some orders, it's not obeying an order if you go along with it when it suits you. Obeying an order means doing so whether it suits you or not, whether it means you're rushing headlong into death. There's not to reason why; there's but to do or die. So that's the acid test. If you would obey the order, even if you were utterly against it, and the EMD failed that acid test completely. So with the EMD when they "complied with orders," to use the Chamber's preferred term, it cannot be said that that amounts to obeying orders; it's just that their will and that of the ABiH sometimes happened to coincide. After all, they were in Bosnia to fight. They weren't there to go on a picnic. Of course they were going to fight. So the crux of the matter is that if they didn't wish to do so, they didn't follow orders. That was indisputably their modus operandi. And so in reality they never obeyed orders, even if sometimes they went along with ABiH tactical plans. I come to the second fundamental error and I'll end on this. For the majority, "the EMD's participation and engagement in the armed conflict against the VRS lies at the core of the determination of Rasim Delic's command and effective control," that's paragraph 461. Now, why should the EMD's participation in the conflict against the VRS lie at the core of its determination? This case didn't concern war crimes committed by the VRS -- sorry, by the EMD in the battle-field. It concerned the treatment of detainees. So surely what lies at the core of the determination of Delic's command and effective control is what happened with prisoners, is what happened with gaining access to prisoners, being able to interview prisoners, find out what's happening to them. So it's almost as if the majority chose the indicator which they thought would give them the most mileage in finding effective control and said that's the core, that's the most important thing. In terms of access to prisoners, the indicators are unequivocally against a finding of effective control. In relation to the EMD's capture of VRS soldiers and their removal to Kamenica camp in July 1995, during Operation Proljece II, the Chamber found that "the EMD did not comply with obligations as set out by the 35th Division Commander concerning the handling of captives taken during combat." Para 403. In other words, the EMD captured and detained the very soldiers who were the subject of this indictment in clear breach of ABiH orders, and in September 1995 again the Chamber found that the EMD detained captives "in defiance," I can't emphasise that strongly enough, "in defiance of the ABiH combat order of Operation Farz." That's paragraph 404 of the trial judgement which stipulated POWs were to be handed over to the military police. And the Chamber further found that the military police had to "act in a consensual manner because the two units were not in a hierarchical relationship," paragraph 405. I'm finishing now. The EMD refused ABiH units access to their camp, in particular to conduct interviews with the captives in the hands of the EMD or to conduct criminal investigations, para 406. The 3rd Corps security service itself reported that "all those captured are under the control of the EMD who do not allow any access to them." That's crucial, they denied access. And see also paragraphs 276 and 281 of the judgement. Yet, it's precisely that lack of access by the ABiH to the detainees which extended even to turning away ABiH security officers, telling them that "there were no detainees," para 410, which meant that the ABiH could not effectively detect and investigate crimes committed by the EMD against the captives. And so nor could Delic. And it's precisely that lack of access which indicates the absence of effective control in that key area, and the majority seriously erred in law when it failed to draw the obvious conclusion resulting in a miscarriage of justice. Thank you, I'm obliged, unless there are any further questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jones. There are no questions from the Judges for the time being. We are therefore going to have a 30-minute break now, and we shall resume at quarter to 12.00, so a little over 30 minutes. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I turn to my fellow Judges to ask them whether they have any questions to put to Mr. Jones. If that's not the case, I'd like to thank you. There's one question from Judge Guney -- you have the floor for your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You submitted your arguments this morning. You developed the key question, i.e., whether Rasim Delic exercised effective control over the MED [as interpreted] extensively. This question ties closely into the -- one of our questions, namely, the fact that Mr. Delic was incriminated under Article 7(3) of the Statute. You did not address this second question very extensively. I would like to know to what extent Rasim Delic was advised of Article 7(3) and the crimes committed by members of the EMD, the fact that he occupied a very high position in the ABiH, to which the EMD was subordinated. Therefore, what connections there were and, more specifically, what role he played and what authority or effective control he exercised. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, insofar as the question related to effective control, I think I've covered the main principles. The fact that Delic occupied a very high position in the ABiH, of course, is not at all a basis in itself to say that therefore there was effective control. That was why I cited from the Halilovic appeals judgement, that it would be simplistic in the extreme to say he was top of the pyramid and therefore he had effective control over the EMD. You -- the -- your question seems to start from the assumption that the EMD was subordinated to the ABiH, but that's precisely what we challenge, if what you're talking about is effective control. They were not under the effective control of the ABiH. That's our whole point. So I'm not sure -- I'm not sure what else really Your Honour would like me to develop in that regard, whether it's a question about de jure, the EMD being de jure subordinated, that's a perhaps sufficiently developed already in our pleadings. But if the key question is effective control, I've addressed that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please open your microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I want to know whether Mr. Delic was advised of the fact that he was being incriminated under Article 7(3) of the Statute for the crimes committed by the EMD, and what role he played in the event that he did have that information in light of the high position he held in the hierarchy of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid, I think as we all see from the transcript, there's a technical difficulty in seeing the question. I heard the first part of the question was, has Mr. Delic been advised that he's been indicted under Article 7(3) of the Statute. If that means advised by us, well, of course he knows he's charged under Article 7(3). As to what Delic did when informed of crimes in light of the, as you say, high position he held, I'm not sure if that's addressed to what our case was or what the Chamber's findings were, or what the Prosecution's case was. It's very difficult to answer a question like that in the abstract. And if the question relates to the third element of command responsibility, taking necessary and reasonable measures, I think we've addressed that at length in our appeals brief and I would simply rely on that and refer the Chamber to what we say there. It would be impossible for me now to recite what action we say Delic took. That would be really re-litigating the whole trial. Sorry. If I have misunderstood, our position clearly is that Delic didn't receive any information about the specific crimes. That's all set out in our appeals brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'd like to thank, Mr. Jones. I shall now give the floor to the Prosecutor so that he can submit his arguments in response to Mr. Delic's arguments. You have 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Todd Schneider appearing for the Prosecution. I will be addressing that General Delic did have effective control in my submissions today. We, of course, are happy to answer questions relating to that General Delic knew or had reason to know of the crime of cruel treatment and that he failed to take the necessary reasonable measures in relation to this crime. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that General Delic had effective control over the El Mujahed Detachment as of July and August 1995, when members of this unit committed the crime of cruel treatment by beating and terrorising a group of a dozen Bosnian Serb prisoners for one month. Because effective control -- because effective control is an evidentiary issue, the Defence must show that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have made this finding. It has failed to do so. I would note that time-lines have been distributed that I will be addressing later on in my submissions. I appreciate the help in distributing those. But before turning to the time-lines, I'm going to start by answering the three questions Your Honours have asked regarding effective control for today. The first, of course, was to elaborate on the indicators of effective control from the Tribunal's jurisprudence that are relevant to determining if a superior does have effective control. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber correctly identified the relevant indicators of effective control for this case at paragraphs 62, 367, and 368 of the judgement. Rather than go through all of these indicators today, I will be focusing more broadly on General Delic's proven ability -- proven material ability to prevent or punish crimes by members of the El Mujahed Detachment, which is of course the definition of effective control. I will further discuss one particular indicator, the ability to issue orders that are followed. Of course I would be happy to discuss any other indicators that you might so wish. The second question was whether any of the indicators of effective control discussed in the judgement are incompatible with the notion of effective control. The answer is no, none of the indicators discussed are incompatible, for two reasons. First, there are no essential, no indispensable indicators of effective control; rather, it is a case-by-case analysis based on the totality of the evidence and that comes from the Strugar appeal judgement, paragraph 254. Second, even particular instances of non-compliance do not necessarily show a lack of control if the other evidence demonstrates that the commander can exercise control when he or she wants to do so. The standard is effective control, not absolute compliance. And of course the example of this is again the Strugar appeals judgement. This case was cited repeatedly earlier by the Defence. However, the Defence has not noted the other important aspect of this judgement. In Strugar the Appeals Chamber upheld a finding that General Strugar had effective control over his troops when they shelled the Old Town of Dubrovnik in December 1991, even though these exact same troops had failed to comply with prior orders not to shell the same location. Strugar appeals judgement 257, 305. These same troops also committed various crimes from October through December 1991, Strugar appeals judgement 257. The Appeals Chamber noted that General Strugar chose not to act regarding these acts of non-compliance. "Where it was important to him, his orders were actually followed." Strugar appeals judgement paragraph 259. The same is true here, General Delic could act where he wanted. The importance of Strugar, the holding of Strugar also is in relation to the Defence's claim that so-called lack of access to prisoners in this case must demonstrate lack of control. I will discuss more fully that there was access to these prisoners early on by other parts of the Bosnian army. But what's important is that we see here -- or we see in Strugar that prior acts of non-compliance for the crime in question - don't shell the Old Town, they shell the Old Town, then they again shell the Old Town - did not preclude a finding of effective control because General Strugar chose not to act. Therefore, any non-compliance in prisoner access in this case, does not necessarily preclude a finding of effective control when the other evidence demonstrates the Trial Chamber was reasonable in its conclusion that General Delic did exercise control given the many other times he and other Bosnian commanders had taken steps. The final question was whether the Trial Chamber erred in concluding and finding that General Delic had effective control over the El Mujahed Detachment as of July and August 1995. The Trial Chamber reasonably found that General Delic did have effective control and the rest of my submissions will elaborate on this answer. In doing so, I'm going to focus on the same two pillars that the Trial Chamber focused on. First, that the El Mujahed Detachment was subordinated to its superior, General Rasim Delic, for two years by the time the crime of cruel treatment occurred in July 1995; second, General Delic had the ability to prevent or punish crimes by members of this unit given the many other times he and other Bosnian army commanders had taken steps to do just that; furthermore, the detachment did comply with orders, particularly those relating to combat. Despite some instances of non-compliance, General Delic still exercised effective control. Turning to the first point, subordination, we of course start with General Delic himself, who, as we know, was the commander of the Main Staff of the Bosnian army, and thereby the most senior officer in the entire army. You see that in paragraphs 99 to 101 of the judgement. When he took over in June 1993, he worked to establish command and control over the entire army, and as the Trial Chamber found, command and control of the army did improve significantly from 1993 to 1995, paragraph 460 of the judgement. The Defence today has asserted there's no evidence to support this finding. We, in our response brief, paragraphs 98 through 109, have set forth the many findings and the detailed evidence that supported this particular finding of improvement of effective control -- of command and control over the army. At this point I would ask you to turn to the first time-line I've distributed entitled "The El Mujahed's Detachment's Subordination to General Rasim Delic." This time-line is based on the findings of the judgement. I will walk through with you each event listed on the time-line, and for ease of reference we've divided those events involving General Delic below the time-line with the rest above. And of course what this time-line shows in total is that the El Mujahed Detachment was subordinated to General Delic for two years -- over two years, starting at the beginning, the beginning of the unit. We see on August 13th, 1993, General Delic authorising the creation of the unit and subordinating them to the 3rd Corps. Prior to this time, there had been requests within the Bosnian army to bring foreign fighters in Central Bosnia into the army. The foreign fighters themselves had specifically made a request that they join the army itself. The Main Staff proposed General Delic that this occur; he agreed. He authorised negotiations which led to the creation of the unit. All of this is discussed at paragraphs 172 to 176 of the judgement. What's important about the formation is that the Bosnian army commanders wanted to incorporate these foreign fighters into the army to achieve command over them and to prevent their unlawful conduct, while the fighters themselves wanted to join to ensure their fighting would be legal, paragraphs 172 to 174. Once a unit is created we see it resubordinated several times over the next two years. It is true the El Mujahed Detachment did not comply with all resubordination orders, that's at paragraph 363 of the judgement. However, we have noted on this time-line the many times they were successfully resubordinated; in September 1993, autumn 1994, and repeatedly throughout 1995, in March, in June, and in September. On top of these many resubordinations, we see the Bosnian army transferring soldiers from other parts of the army into the El Mujahed Detachment. We see that in October 1994, in August 1995. As we note in our response brief, paragraph 70, they transferred approximately 86 soldiers into the unit, a significant number. They also resubordinated the 5th Manoeuvre Battalion to the El Mujahed Detachment, as noted on September 11th, 1995. As the Trial Chamber noted, this transfer of soldiers into the unit, this resubordination of units to the detachment, shows that the unit was within the hierarchy of the Bosnian army. The commanders would not have been abandoning control of so many soldiers by sending them apart to a separate entity, paragraph 467. Finally, we see the events relating to the disbandment of the unit at the end of the time-line. On December 12th, 1995, General Delic ordering that the unit be disbanded. A few days later, the 3rd Corps issuing its order on the same topic. The unit is disbanded, and on January 1st, 1996, we see the Bosnian army hosting a farewell for this unit, attended by General Delic himself. Apart from all these many events in the time-line, we have the findings throughout the judgement that the Bosnian army commanders issued dozens of orders to this unit. Many of them are collected at footnote 1183 of the judgement. These orders relate to combat, redeployment, reporting, and other subjects. We are not suggesting that they complied with all these orders; rather, we are raising in the context of subordination that the high volume of orders issued to this unit and the fact that they were continually issued throughout the two-year time-span of the unit's existence, in particular in 1995, shows again that the El Mujahed Detachment was within the hierarchy of the Bosnian army.
