It would have been illogical for Bosnian army commanders to issue so many orders to a unit that wasn't part of their structure. All that I've discussed shows that the Trial Chamber was reasonable in finding that the El Mujahed Detachment was subordinated to General Delic for two years, and particularly July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [In English] You will agree with me that the question of treatment of prisoners is very central to this appeal. And I would be very grateful if you would in the course of your argument explain to the Bench how does EMD's lack of co-operation with regard to the handling of prisoners impact on the convictions entered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours. I would turn to that right now. I would start, though, by saying, as I hope to develop further, all the evidence demonstrated the reasonableness of the Trial Chamber's finding regarding many areas of control. With regard to the issue of prisoners, it is true that the El Mujahed Detachment did deny access sometimes to prisoners it held into its camp, but at the same time they handed over some prisoners immediately, paragraph 403 of the judgement. They also handed over other prisoners eventually, albeit in an untimely manner, including the particular victim prisoners from July 1995, and that's paragraph 283. Moreover, they did provide access to the prisoners subjected to cruel treatment from July. This occurred almost as soon as they were captured and it resulted in detailed interviews gathering intelligence from the prisoners, which was the focus of the access. And this may be found in paragraphs 274 to 275, 282, and 549. Therefore, when the Defence has asserted today that it was impossible to gain access to the detainees, at page 32, that's not correct based on the findings of the judgement. Apart from this specific prisoner issue, I would note that Bosnian army soldiers and commanders entered the camps at other times, paragraphs 411 and 431. Furthermore, there were lots of meetings between members of the El Mujahed Detachment and their superiors in the Bosnian army. Many of these are noted between paragraphs 427 and 433 of the judgement. This shows the El Mujahed Detachment was available regarding these prisoners. They were not hidden away with no way to get in touch with them and no idea where they might be. It would have been easy to get in touch with the prison -- with the El Mujahed Detachment further regarding these prisoners rather than just seek to interview them for intelligent purposes. And I would just note at this point that the fact that there were many meetings between the El Mujahed Detachment and their superiors in the Bosnian army refutes the Defence's assertion or reliance on one witness who says it was very difficult to reach the detachment. One particular piece of evidence does not undermine the reasonableness of the Trial Chamber's findings that there was repeated contact, communication, and meetings between the El Mujahed Detachment and their superiors. Returning for a moment to the question of subordination in general, not only was it reasonable for the Trial Chamber to find that there was subordination. All of the evidence I've talked about shows the Defence has failed to show that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in rejecting its theories of co-operation and outside control. First, with respect to co-operation, this is not a case about co-operation or mere influence. As the Trial Chamber noted and as the Defence has also cited earlier today, co-operation involves separate, independent entities rather than a single military structure. Co-operation involves mutual agreement rather than the issuing of orders. And this is all from paragraphs 345, 349, and 350 of the judgement. The Defence asked today: Is there any finding in the judgement inconsistent with co-operation? Of course there is. If you're co-operating with somebody, if you're co-ordinating with another unit, you don't create the unit, you don't disband the unit, you don't issue dozens of orders to the unit, you don't transfer soldiers into the unit, you don't assign them a headquarters, you don't promote members of the unit, you don't give members awards, you don't issue them passports, you don't grant them permission to travel abroad, as General Delic personally did, paragraph 422 of the judgement; you don't repeatedly investigate the unit, as I'll discuss more in a moment. These are the hallmarks of a subordinated unit. As for the Defence's theory of outside control, yes, the El Mujahed Detachment did receive financial and logistical support from local authorities, paragraph 441. They received financial support and were in communication with private foreign institutions, paragraph 442. This support and communication, though, was not evidence of control by these outsiders, nor did any of this interfere with the control exercised by the Bosnian army over its subordinate unit, the El Mujahed Detachment. The Defence's focus on theoretical control by others ignores the actual control exercised by General Delic and the Bosnian army commanders. At this point I would turn from the issue of subordination to General Delic's material ability to prevent or punish crimes, and in doing so I would refer to the second time-line that we've distributed. Again, this time-line is based on the findings of the judgement. I'll walk you through each of the events listed on the chart, and we have divided this chart so that measures relating to prevention are below the time-line and those relating to punishment are above. Before actually going into the particulars of this chart, though, I do want to correct an assertion by the Defence that the question is the ability to prevent or punish war crimes. No. That limitation is not in the Tribunal's jurisprudence; rather, it is preventing or punishing crimes by one's subordinates. And here we see ample examples of this. First, with regard to prevention, we see in December 1993, General Delic himself ordering a "clamp-down" on the El Mujahed Detachment and another unit. In spring 1995 we see General Delic again getting involved to personally authorise Operation Vranduk, designed to curb illegal activities by members of the unit. Around the same time, April 12th, 1995, General Delic, on a report of "unacceptable activities" by members of the El Mujahed Detachment, writes on a report to the security administration "proposal to finally resolve this." Moving on, in July 1995, we see after an investigation by military security into threats made by members of the unit against a shop owner, military security announcing they will take measures to prevent such incidents. And finally, in December 1995, an admission by a member of the El Mujahed Detachment that: "The army today prevented us from attacking Zepce for revenge." At the same time, throughout these two years, we see steps related to punishment. We see two members of the El Mujahed Detachment arrested in February 1994 for the murder of Paul Goodall, a British humanitarian worker. Proceedings are initiated. However, they later escape. Contrary to any suggestion by the Defence, this was not merely a civilian exercise, but rather a joint military effort to arrest these men. Throughout 1995, again of course critical, in this case we see military security investigating members of the El Mujahed Detachment again and again; in January for abduction and mistreatment, on May 23rd for torture, on May 26th for desecrating a cemetery, in July for threats against a Bosnian army soldier. The Defence has raised these threats many times this morning without noting the resulting investigation into this particular incident. Finally, in October 1995, we see criminal proceedings again initiated against a member of the El Mujahed Detachment, this time for theft. All of these examples show General Delic's material ability to prevent or punish crimes by members of the El Mujahed Detachment. The Defence is incorrect when it suggests you only focus on what General Delic did as opposed to what his subordinates did as well when examining -- when reviewing the reasonableness of the Trial Chamber's finding that General Delic had the ability to prevent and punish crimes, either by acting himself or through his subordinates, which is typical of someone in his high power. An incident that's not mentioned on this time-line but that was highlighted by Defence this morning relates to the 35th Division asking for help from local authorities in relation to misconduct by members of the unit. At paragraph 441 of the judgement. The significance of this request is that it again shows the fact that Bosnian army commanders, General Delic, if necessary through his subordinates, could act either alone as evidenced by the many times on this time-line military security itself had taken steps, or with the help of civilian authorities, in paragraph 441 and again is referenced in arresting the suspected murders for Paul Goodall. There are multiple options available for preventing or punishing crimes by this unit. Furthermore, all the steps listed on this time-line, investigations, arrests, and others, show that contrary to the Defence's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to ask you to slow down, please, because it is difficult for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: I apologise. All of the events discussed in this time-line, the investigations, the arrests, the criminal proceedings, show that the Defence was not correct when it asserted even this morning that use of force was the only option. There were many other proven steps available to General Delic, in respect specifically to July 1995 and in general in demonstrating his ability to prevent and punish crimes. So these many examples show the Trial Chamber's finding was reasonable that General Delic could prevent or punish crimes. It further shows that the Defence was wrong when it claimed it was impossible for General Delic and others to act. We know that it was a choice not to act rather than any impossibility, given the many other times highlighted on this time-line that General Delic and other Bosnian army commanders had taken steps to prevent or punish crimes by members of the El Mujahed Detachment. All this further shows that the following is not true, that the El Mujahed Detachment had a propensity to violence if it was confronted, that confronting the El Mujahed Detachment would start a war on a third front, this is noted in Judge Moloto's dissenting opinion, paragraphs 8 and 9, raised again by the Defence questioning the Trial Chamber's finding in paragraph 468 that these broad claims of violence were not credible. The Trial Chamber's rejection of these broad claims of a third front or violence was reasonable based on the findings in evidence before it, based on the many times highlighted on this time-line where General Delic and other Bosnian army commanders had taken steps to prevent or punish crimes without any violent third front reaction. The question arises: If the Bosnian army could take steps in general, why didn't they in July and August 1995 regarding the specific crime of cruel treatment? The answer is: Military expediency. They prioritised the El Mujahed Detachment's compliance with combat orders over its misconduct in other areas. First in this regard is Exhibit 583, an August 30th military security report. The judgement quotes this partially in footnote 1159. We've quoted it more fully in our response brief at paragraph 39. In the context of talking about repeated misconduct by members of the El Mujahed Detachment, military security reports: "No energetic measures have been taken so that the relations with this unit would not be spoiled and that combat operations would be carried out as successfully as possible." The timing of this is key. It is right after the crime of cruel treatment in this case has ended, in August 1995, and right before the Bosnian army will launch Operation Farz and Uragan, in September 1995, during which the El Mujahed Detachment will play a key role in helping them achieve one of the top military objectives of the Bosnian army. Now, it's true that Exhibit 583 also contains broad claim that the El Mujahed Detachment "has operated independently and has not respected the control and command system." The Defence has cited this in its reply brief at paragraph 19. We had already noted the same language in footnote 114 of our response brief. Importantly, the Trial Chamber viewed this broad claim skeptically and did so reasonably given all the specific evidence of control and the ability to prevent and punish already discussed, as well as the fact within the same report, on the same page, military security says the El Mujahed Detachment "has completed all the assigned military tasks." We don't control them, but they do everything we ask them to do. It just doesn't make sense. Similar in this regard is Exhibit 938, an exhibit the Defence has actually highlighted today earlier in its submissions. This is a July 5th, 1995, military security report. It relates to the investigation into the El Mujahed Detachment's threats against fellow Bosnian army soldiers that was discussed extensively earlier by the Defence and that I noted already on our time-line. This particular exhibit is noted in 1162 of the judgement. And the report demonstrates -- report shows that after conducting its investigation and determining that these threats were made, military security met with threatened soldiers and "tried to console them, telling them that they were prepared to do everything requested by members of the above-mentioned unit," clearly the El Mujahed Detachment, "in order to execute planned assignments, i.e., occupy Paljenik and Vozuca." As I'd mentioned with regard to the prior exhibit, Vozuca was this key, top military objective of the Bosnian army, paragraph 86 of the judgement, that was successfully captured in September 1995, and Paljenik, as mentioned in the report, was the "gateway to enter the Vozuca pocket," paragraph 398. There is nothing in these two exhibits about it being impossible to crack down on the El Mujahed Detachment. Rather, what the reports -- what military security is saying is: Hold off on doing anything because we need them to succeed in combat. And how did the commanders in the Bosnian army know that they would achieve this military success with the El Mujahed Detachment? Because, quite simply, they knew that the El Mujahed Detachment did follow orders, particularly those relating to combat. As the Trial Chamber found, the Bosnian army controlled the El Mujahed Detachment's participation in and engagement in combat, paragraph 461. Importantly, the El Mujahed Detachment never fought without authorisation from its superiors in the Bosnian army, paragraphs 386 and 465. We see especially in the combat operations surrounding the July 1995 crime of cruel treatment, the El Mujahed Detachment repeatedly following orders relating to combat. In May 1995, in Operation Proljece, where they spear head an attack as ordered. In July 1995, in Operation Proljece II, where they are the primary leader of the attack and they follow various orders to attack. And finally, in what I've mentioned before, Operations Farz and Uragan, in September 1995, where they again followed various orders to attack. And all of this is referenced in the trial judgement paragraphs 394 to 402. Now, it is true, as noted in the judgement and highlighted by the Defence, that there was some non-compliance with combat orders, but we need to understand the process by which this happened. First, the El Mujahed Detachment's questioning orders from its superiors was part of the general process within the Bosnian army of planning operations in general, paragraphs 377 to 379. Specifically, the Trial Chamber found that this dialectical relationship applied to the El Mujahed Detachment and its superiors in the Bosnian army, paragraph 465. There were a few times when the El Mujahed Detachment refused to participate in attacks at the time they had been ordered. This was not: We won't go and fight, we sit on our hands for no reason whatsoever. Rather, not carrying out the attack at this time was a reasoned decision by the detachment that they shared with their superiors. Either the unit itself or battle-field conditions were not ready for the attacks at the time they were ordered, paragraphs 388 to 390 of the judgement. As the Trial Chamber found, their superiors in the Bosnian army agreed with the El Mujahed Detachment's assessment, because two of the three attacks were carried out at a later time and the third was cancelled. 388 to 390 of the judgement. Importantly, no steps or sanctions were taken against the El Mujahed Detachment for this non-compliance, paragraph 462 of the judgement. And just to respond to a point raised by the Defence earlier, when the detachment said that battle-field conditions were not ready, for example, because the leaves had fallen, this was not a "joke," but rather, this was an important consideration that there was no foliage, no trees, leaves, available to hide the attackers and they would have been open to the enemy combatants. And in this respect I would refer you to transcript pages 66 to 67 of Witness Awad from the Sarajevo hearing. But what is important about these delays in fighting was that it ended at the latest by March 1995. The El Mujahed Detachment fought pursuant to orders throughout May to September 1995, again right around the time of cruel treatment in July 1995. Moreover, this non-compliance is very different from the ability to prevent or punish crimes. In fact, many of the examples highlighted by the Defence of alleged non-compliance don't show any interference with the superior's ability to prevent or punish crimes. Yes, they set up camp 13 kilometres away from Zavidovici instead of 12. Yes, they refused to comply with many paperwork requirements that were highlighted earlier today at paragraph 373 of the judgement. These don't conflict with the actual examples of prevention and punishment that I've already discussed today. Even the question of reporting. First, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that the El Mujahed Detachment's oral reporting partly compensated for its failure to submit written reports as ordered, paragraph 463 of the judgement. And perhaps going to a question raised by Judge Meron earlier, when it came to the fact that while subordinated to the 35th Division the El Mujahed Detachment did report directly above the 35th Division to the 3rd Corps is entirely consistent that at the same time, again while the detachment is under the 35th Division, the 3rd Corps is directly ordering the El Mujahed Detachment itself. And that's at paragraph 431 of the judgement. So it would be unsurprising that the detachment was reporting directly in September 1995 to a commander that was at the same time giving its orders. But frankly, what's important about this question of reporting at what level is that in the end General Delic was above 35th Division and the 3rd Corps, and any question of who was reported to below him did not affect the flow of information up and the flow of orders down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Judge Meron has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. [In English] Now supposing that there was broad compliance with orders pertaining to combat, could that not be explained on the basis of tactical co-operation rather than on the basis of a command structure? And I wish you would be as specific with regard to compliance with orders not plaining to combat but with respect to treatment of people, particularly POWs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: In -- under the facts of this case, the compliance with orders was yet further evidence of the subordination of the El Mujahed Detachment to its superiors rather than examples of co-operation. Given, as I'd mentioned before, the many other steps related to this unit, creating it, disbanding it, promoting members, giving them awards, investigating them, if you're just going to co-operate with another unit, you're not going to bother going through all those steps. As far as its compliance with orders relating to treatment of prisoners of war, in the first respect -- as again I'd mentioned there was direct access to those prisoners quickly, of course if there had been no violations of how to treat the prisoners of war, there would be no case today. Apart from that, we do see the El Mujahed Detachment treating other prisoners properly, correctly, as they are required to do under the laws of war in handing them over immediately at paragraph 403 of the judgement. If I could return briefly to the topic of reporting. Any questions about reporting problems in the end, again, doesn't interfere with an ability to prevent or punish crimes when there are the many examples of this occurring at other times and these particular reporting problems aren't interfering with knowledge of further crimes by members of the El Mujahed Detachment. In particular, in respect to the July prisoners subjected to the cruel treatment, other parts of the Bosnian army knew immediately of the situation despite any "reporting problems," and that's paragraphs 274 to 282. What the Defence seeks to do is to use a magnifying glass to highlight a problem here, look only at a problem there. The proper -- the Trial Chamber properly examined the entire picture, the totality of the circumstances, and in particular looked at all the events from 1993 to 1995 rather than just isolated incidents, paragraph 370. The Defence has mentioned today, many times, the appeals judgement in Hadzihasanovic. Your Honours, the El Mujahed Detachment in the Hadzihasanovic case from October 1993 was a very different unit than the El Mujahed Detachment of this case in July 1995. And this, of course, relates to a question Judge Liu had raised earlier. This key two-year time difference is reflected in the many examples of subordination and control I've already discussed today. In this case as well, there actually was a finding of a lack of control back in 1993 relating to a predecessor of this unit. In this regard I would also refer to or note that the Defence cited, from paragraph 381 of the judgement, a report from the unit that they are not part -- considering themselves part of the Bosnian army. This again is from November 1993, almost two years away from the crime of cruel treatment in July 1995. There are many other significant differences between the El Mujahed Detachment of Hadzihasanovic and this case. First, there were almost no orders issued to the unit in Hadzihasanovic. Only three are discussed at paragraphs 199 to 200 of the judgement [sic]. Here, of course, dozens of orders were issued to the El Mujahed Detachment. In Hadzihasanovic it was noted that communication and contact with the El Mujahed Detachment was difficult and that there were almost no investigations of members of this unit, paragraphs 211, 218, and 219. Here, communication was easy, given the many meetings between the El Mujahed Detachment and its superiors, given the access provided to the camp and prisoners at times. Furthermore, given the many investigations, criminal proceedings, and other steps taken in response to crimes or misconduct by members of the unit that are detailed in this case. Finally, in Hadzihasanovic, Bosnian army commanders repeatedly took steps, issuing orders, issuing threats, to try to free the prisoners that were being held. Here all they did was take steps to interview the prisoners and gather detailed intelligence. In sum, Your Honours, the El Mujahed Detachment was subordinate to its superior General Rasim Delic for two years by July 1995. Furthermore, General Delic had the proven material ability to prevent or punish crimes by members of this unit, given the many times such steps had been taken. It was therefore reasonable for the Trial Chamber to find that General Delic did have effective control. The Defence has failed to show otherwise. It has instead focused on broad claims rather than noting the specific findings in evidence. We therefore respectfully request that Defence's challenges in particular to effective control in ground 1 be dismissed, and that would conclude my submissions on that point. Thank you. Unless there are any questions either on this point or on the other two issues, grounds, in which case we would ask that you dismiss those grounds of appeal as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Schneider. Are there any questions from the Judges? Yes, Judge Liu has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for providing us with the time-line and your comments on the differences between the two cases, that is, the Hadzihasanovic case and this case. I just want to know what is your position on the reply given by the Defence counsel to my question this morning in which Mr. Jones, if I'm not mistaken, alleges that the Trial Chamber committed an error in not substantiating or giving any reasons to its finding that the command and control were improved significantly from 1993 to 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: If I might have a moment to consult before I answer, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. Your Honour, in paragraphs 98 to 109 of our response brief we highlight many of the findings showing improvement in the command/control generally in the Bosnian army. I would highlight in particular the fact that in paragraphs 287 -- I'm sorry, that's my footnote, in paragraph 460 it is noted that general functioning regarding planning and preparation of combat orders had improved, in part because of General Delic's efforts to improve the system of command and control. And again in the same paragraph, that loyalty difficulties encountered when General Delic originally took over had been addressed. Furthermore, importantly, as noted in paragraphs 136 and 137, General Delic authorised several specific operations "to remove obstacles to the functioning of the Bosnian army system of command and control." All of these steps and many other evidence demonstrated the reasonableness of the Trial Chamber's finding that the command and control over the army generally had improved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you mean that the Trial Chamber did not commit an error because all the reasonings are scattered everywhere in the judgement and taking into the overall, total evidence all-together?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: That is a much answer, if I may say, and to the point, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Schneider, if I understood you correctly, you said a few minutes ago that in contrast to Hadzihasanovic, Delic and others in this case did nothing with regard to getting really involved in this question of prisoners. Now, there was -- paragraph 403 of the judgement indicates that there was a standing order of the 35th Division commander concerning handling of captives and that all -- and according to this order, prisoners were to be brought in to the nearest security unit and then to the 35th Division. Now -- so there were orders to move the prisoners to a central command where presumably they would be under better protection. Now, I understand that this order was not executed. What can we learn from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: I would focus on two points in answering that question. First, there was some compliance with this order, as noted in the same paragraph. They did immediately hand over some prisoners. Furthermore, such general orders relating broadly would not be sufficient in the context of necessary or reasonable measures to show that this would be sufficient in response to the actual information, alarming information, that was passed throughout the Bosnian army and up to General Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose that the Defence would later point out if there was a more specific order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Pocar has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I tried to understand exactly how the situation was in fact, because many of arguments went to the de jure subordination, and on that we can perhaps easily agree. But what is relevant is the de facto subordination that amounts to really effective control, which of course has to be proven beyond reasonable doubt. One cannot rely on the de jure subordination which forces an indicator maybe of the effective control is one of the indicators but cannot be the basic indicator alone. And I'm referring essentially to the -- your answer to the question put by Judge Liu, the impression one gets that efforts were made by Delic to make effective a control which originally was not and originally was not as it's proven by the Hadzihasanovic case. There was no real control of the ABiH army over the EMD, but efforts were made to make the control effective. Where are we exactly? I mean, did these efforts make the control fully effective, is that your position, that the control was made fully effective as a consequence of these acts so that the only reasonable conclusion that the Trial Chamber could reach was that indeed the efforts succeeded; or is there still a margin of doubt? Because you said some prisoners were handed over, some were not. Was it fully -- fully effective, the control, in your view? Because we have to remove any margin of doubt. You are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: If I may consult for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCHNEIDER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the finding of effective control is a factual finding in this case, as in many other cases, and therefore the standard to review is whether the Trial Chamber was reasonable. The evidence and findings demonstrate the reasonableness. Turning first to the de jure subordination, that of course can be and in this case happened -- was a prima facie indicator of effective control, as is consistent with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. Furthermore, the many steps taken following the initial creation, the resubordination from here to here which they complied with, transfer of orders, the fact that a unit disbanded when ordered, these not only relate to subordination narrowly, but to generally effective control over the entire unit and of course compliance with orders. As far as, again, the Hadzihasanovic case, the findings in this case relate to entire two-year period, much of which, of course, would not be in the Hadzihasanovic case, which focused on October 1993. And during 1994 and 1995 we see repeated compliance with combat orders, repeated investigations of the members of the unit, them being subjected to criminal proceedings. Therefore, the findings generally that command and control improve significantly over the entire Bosnian army as well as the fact that by July 1995 General Delic had effective control over the El Mujahed Detachment was reasonable based on the evidence before the Trial Chamber. And if I may add one more point to that. Of course it's not absolute compliance, full control; it's effective control. And the Strugar appeals judgement demonstrates that certain acts of non-compliance, even relating to the particular issue crime in question, did not show a lack of effective control; rather, it must be - and the Trial Chamber did here - an analysis of all the evidence of whether the commander was choosing not to act which was the case there and is the case here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Schneider. The Defence may now proceed with their reply. You have 20 minutes to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In terms of the schedule, in fact I was going to suggest that if we're not continuing after the lunch break that we might have a comfort break, as it's sometimes colloquially referred, just for five minutes, otherwise I can continue. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If it's a difficulty, I can press on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged. Thank you. Well, if I could start firstly in response to a matter raised by Judge Meron, he referred the Prosecutor to paragraph 403 of the judgement. And the Prosecutor replied that insofar as that was concerned, there was partial compliance because some detainees were released. Well, those were captured Bosnian Muslims. They're not even prisoners of war at all. So there's no compliance at all because the order concerns prisoners, not civilians who have just -- civilian -- Bosnian Muslim civilians who had simply got in the way. And you asked whether there were any other orders. Well, paragraph 404 goes on to refer to another order which was defied by the EMD, and so that's -- obviously that's pertinent too. Now, responding to the Prosecution's submissions, the Prosecution repeatedly said how the Trial Chamber found effective control. Well, that's of course completely wrong. It's not the Chamber, it's only two Judges, with Judge Moloto dissenting, and the Judges themselves were clear about that. And it's worth reflecting that 2-1 vote is a very small margin. Translated into a jury trial that would be 8 to 4, which I think isn't acceptable in any common law jurisdiction. But be that as it may, it's allowed under the Statute, but one swing vote means that a man's fate hangs on a very slender thread. My learned friend also referred repeatedly to what was reasonable in terms of conclusions by the Chamber. That -- the assessment of reasonableness has to be seen in the context of what the Chamber itself said about a case based on circumstantial evidence. And you'll see at paragraph 28 where the Chamber reminded itself: "It is not sufficient that it is," it being guilt, "a reasonable conclusion available from that evidence. It must be the only reasonable conclusion available. If there is another conclusion which is also reasonably open from that evidence and which is consistent with the innocence of the accused, he must be acquitted." So the point I make is it's not enough if one says: Well, the majority's view was one reasonable view. It's only if their view was one open to them only on the basis that it was the only reasonable conclusion. And we say, of course, that it wasn't. Now, I'm going to deal as much as I can in an orderly manner with my learned friend's submissions, but of course when one replies, it's not always possible to have a completely logical progression. I'll start with the issue of resubordination and the orders on resubordination. In fact, the orders on resubordination show the complete opposite of what the Prosecution thinks. They say the orders on resubordination were successful. Well, that's their gloss on it. All that we have is evidence of many orders on resubordination. And the reason why there were many is precisely because it was unsuccessful. They weren't succeeding to resubordinate the unit. And we've referred to this at paragraph 25 in our appeals brief. One sees that in six days the EMD was issued three orders on subordination or resubordination and that it didn't follow any of these orders, and that's the evidence of PW-9. So they weren't issuing lots of resubordination orders because it was such a success. It's the complete opposite. They had to keep trying because it wasn't working. And here perhaps I can deal also with the issue of improvement, the notion that there was improvement. And I think I have to ask to go into closed session because there's an exhibit which is under seal which I just want to call up. I believe that e-court is able to call up exhibits and it's E 661, but of course if they can refrain from calling it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, dealing with the first time-line, we see Delic authorising the creation of the EMD. Well, I won't call up the relevant exhibit, given the shortness of time, but it's E 273, which shows firstly this was a proposal by the RBiH and that Delic was not out of his own personal authority creating the EMD. And it's well established in the Tribunal's case law that merely being a conduit through which your superior passes an order doesn't place you in a position of effective control. And at the end of that exhibit there are a list of things which had to happen in order for the EMD to be established. It had to provide a list of its members, it had to report on what it had done, and none of that -- none of that happened. So right from the start it didn't actually work out, and that's clear from the evidence, and if we have time I'll provide the reference to our -- where that's dealt with in our Defence appeals brief. The Prosecution says that Delic replenished the unit, but in fact as we see from the judgement, joining the EMD was even treated as desertion, paragraph 174. In terms of all the orders which were issued and which they rely -- the Prosecution rely very heavily on footnote 1183, which is indeed key for the majority as being all the orders -- a whole list of orders which were issued to the EMD, combat orders. You'll notice very significantly in that paragraph that there are no references to transcripts at all, no references to witness evidence. And so significantly, there's no evidence that those orders were complied with. In fact, these are just exhibits which mentioned the EMD on it. And that's why, as I say, very significantly, that there's absolutely not a single transcript reference in that whole footnote. Besides, this was co-operation with tactical parts of the combat orders, that's the Chamber's own words at 461, and so we say consistent anyway with co-operation. As for disbandment, again relied on as creating and disbanding the unit, well, if we see paragraph 198 of the judgement, and I'll ask you to simply turn that up, it's a matter which we've dealt with in our appeals briefs, one sees this: "According to a former EMD member, without the surest consent the EMD would have continued fighting." So in any event, disbandment hinged on the shura agreeing. It wasn't because Delic ordering it. And as we all know, this is in the context of the Dayton Peace Agreement which provided that all foreigners had to leave the territory. So it was in that context that this happened. My learned friend went through a list of the facts which he said were incompatible with co-operation, and he listed, for example, promoting members, appointing members to the EMD by the ABiH. Well, you'll see at paragraph 191 of the judgement that there were no ranks in the EMD. So the notion that actually appointing or promoting people is fairly meaningless, particularly given that the leaders were not appointed by the ABiH. That's paragraph 187 of the trial judgement. In terms of issuing awards, my learned friend says, well, that's never done in terms of allied armies; well, quite the contrary. I won't mention that my grandfather, an American colonel, got the OBE from the UK for his wartime services. He wasn't under the effective control of the UK. James Stewart, the American actor, received a Croix de Guerre from France. No one would say he was under the effective control of the French. That is certainly something which allied armies can do and do do. So it's, if anything, a very weak indicator, if it's an indicator at all, of effective control. The second time-line refers to the Goodall case. Really, it's sufficient to look at what the Chamber itself said about that at paragraph 448. Exhibit E 887 sets out all of what we rely on in that regard. But it's plain from the judgement itself, proceedings were instituted before a civilian court and they were never even concluded. So as to what one can draw from that, we say very little, and they subsequently escaped. My learned friend says that it's not correct to say that the use of force was not the only option, and they develop this theory which I don't see the majority is developing particularly, but that there was a question of military expediency, that the ABiH had sort of decided to do a pact with the devil and not confront them because they were so useful. In fact, as we've seen, far from being useful, the EMD, for example, meant that they couldn't send Catholic or Orthodox soldiers to the front. But what they refer to in support of that very thin submission is footnote 1159. But it's not Delic who made the remark about not taking energetic measures in order not to spoil relations, it's the 35th Division. And so that's significant. It can't be held against him that someone expressed that view. And to the contrary, he was in fact in favour of confronting, violently, if necessary, the EMD. And we've set that out in our appeals brief at paragraph 383, that in fact there was a division within the ABiH of how to deal with the EMD. And Delic was actually in favour of taking strong action, but it was said - and this is Witness Karavelic - any attempt that General Delic took on his own to disarm them would have inevitably had led to loss of life among civilians. "He did not have the right to do that from the Supreme Command." So that's very significant. He in fact, had it been in his power to do so, would have taken action. So he certainly can't be charged with accepting the EMD for military expediency. The Prosecution referred to E 583, showing that the EMD had completed all its tasks. Well, obviously what one has to see is that exhibit in context. Time doesn't allow it, but if we look at E 583, obviously the phrase "has completed all assigned military tasks" has to be read in context. The Prosecution referred to the dialectical approach and the idea that what the EMD did what a normal dialectic with superior commands, but that simply misunderstands what Dr. Paul Cornish, the expert who introduced the expression, was referring to. You find it at paragraph 379 of the judgement. And what he says is that: Yes, you have an exchange of ideas, but where there's effective control in essence at the end the commander says: Thank you for your contribution, but this is how we're going to do it. And that's not how it went with the EMD. That's the critical distinction. If there was this exchange and they EMD said: No, we don't want to fight for this and this reason, they wouldn't accept an ABiH commander saying: Well, tough luck, you have to do it. And that's critical. And they and the majority misunderstood that. My learned friend has referred to Strugar on which they rely, it seems, quite heavily. A very different case obviously. Strugar involved regular army units, a fundamentally different proposition from foreign fighters with the extremist views, bizarre and erratic behaviour of the shura, the Emir, the foreign supporters. It really is barely worth comparing the two. Forgive me. Just, I think, two other matters. With respect to Delic being informed of measures taken against the EMD, which is highlighted in the time-lines, certainly there was an attempt to have information to clarify what was happening with the EMD, but that isn't tantamount to effective control. It's only human, it's only normal, you're going to try and find out what's happening with this unit. But the crucial point is the ABiH couldn't liaise with the EMD in order to carry out proper investigations because the EMD had their own superiors and they didn't have security officers or intelligence officers. And that's precisely the organ which deals with crimes being committed and investigation. And that's clear from paragraph 425 of the trial judgement, where you see that the assistant commander for security -- sorry, in the words of one witness: "Each battalion had a security organ, brigades had a security organ, and the division had a security organ. The exception to this was the EMD, which -- with which we never established contacts with respect to the security organ." And so that was what was preventing anything from really happening. You'll see Awad as well, at paragraph 192, says that officially his title was security officer but he just acted as an interpreter. So it's hopeless. Without the EMD having security intelligence organs it wasn't possible to properly investigate. And what's more, because they didn't provide a list of the identities of their members, they didn't know who was even in the EMD. So how do you investigate a crime maybe committed by the EMD if you don't even know who was in the unit? They also, the EMD, besides submitting - and you'll see in the evidence a list of their members only with nationalities, Kuwait, Iran, Pakistan, the names left blank, they also didn't have any military identification documents, that's paragraph 191, again making proper security and intelligence investigation work impossible. And finally, on prisoners Prosecution say: Well, yes, the ABiH did get access eventually to the prisoners. Well, that's certainly not true of the September prisoners who were simply killed by the EMD. The ABiH in fact had to leave the camp of the EMD because of fear for their own safety. And you'll see that at paragraph 275 of the judgement, where -- relates to how the assistant commanders of the 35th Division went to see the VRS detainees. "When Imamovic asked the detainees about the circumstances of their capture, an armed Mujahedin appeared and started yelling in a foreign language. Out of concern for their own safety, the two ABiH soldiers left." Again, that's very significant. It's not just slight difficulties in gaining access. They're running out of the camp for fear that they're going to be killed or injured by the EMD. Again, how does that equate to effective control? And yes, the Prosecution gave examples of how sometimes access was given to the camp, but it's very significant what that was for. It was clearly for religious propaganda purposes. You see at paragraph 411 they would allow other members into the camp in order to pray together. They were probably recruiting. It would be quite a good way to get new members. So one has to see the context. We do say that access to the detainees and the camp is critical in a case of this nature. Otherwise, one can imagine this reductio ad absurdum. Let's imagine not the facts of this case, I emphasise, but let's imagine the EMD complied absolutely with combat orders without fail, but conversely they would fight to the last man before they would give access to their camps. It's not that far, the latter anyway, from the facts in this case. How, then, would that be a basis for saying that an accused should have done something, could have done something about detainees? Again, it's a non sequitur. What has combat got to do with whether there was effective control in relation to these crimes? And finally, Hadzihasanovic was not distinguished purely on the basis that Hadzihasanovic only issued three orders, here there were many. That's an over-simplistic way of distinguishing that case from this. But in any event, I think you have our submissions and unless I can assist you further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We thank you, Mr. Jones. We shall now have a one-hour break and resume at 20 minutes past 2.00 p.m. and hear the Prosecution's appeal. We shall resume at half past 2.00. The court stands adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.20 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you all. The court is back in session. We shall now give the floor to the Prosecutor so that he may present his appeal. You have one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For 35 days in the summer of 1995, General Rasim Delic's subordinates, members of the El Mujahed Detachment, humiliated and terrorised 11 prisoners of war. General Delic, as you heard earlier today, formed the El Mujahed Detachment out of a group of violent foreigners. Not only did he create this unit, he tolerated their criminal behaviour for two years before the prisoners of war at issue in this case fell into their hands. When the war ended, General Delic disbanded the unit and thanked and praised its members for their service. General Delic's three-year sentence fails to reflect both the gravity of the "appallingly brutal" crimes at issue here and the gravity of his failure to prevent and punish the crimes of members of the El Mujahed Detachment. The sentence lacks any deterrent value to dissuade future commanders to choose, as General Delic did in this case, military expediency over an obligation to enforce international humanitarian law. As such, the sentence attracts the condemnation of the international community. The Appeals Chamber should revise this manifestly inadequate sentence and impose a more appropriate sentence of seven years' imprisonment. The path leading to the abuse and terrorisation of these 11 prisoners of war in July 1995 starts in Central Bosnia in 1993. On June 13th, 1993, one of General Delic's subordinate commanders told him: "In the general area of Zenica municipality since the beginning of the war, there have been volunteers from foreign countries who have not entered the BH army." And that: "In fighting to date, they have been acting outside the usual context and lawful methods of combat, which is detrimental to the BH state, and especially to the RBiH army." That's from trial judgement 172. As a solution to this problem, General Delic's subordinate commanders proposed that these foreigners should either be sent back to where they came from or organised into a unit, and that's at trial judgement 173. General Delic acted quickly on this request, and on the 13th of August he signed an order "authorising the formation of a detachment named El Mujahedin" composed of "foreign volunteers currently on the territory of the 3rd Corps zone of responsibility." That's at trial judgement 177. This is the El Mujahed Detachment. After this unit was formed, General Delic was "informed via bulletins sent by the Security Administration of numerous instances of misconduct involving the El Mujahed Detachment members, some of which amounted to criminal offences." This is at trial judgement 501, which lists a number of instances in which General Delic was put on notice of criminal behaviour of the El Mujahed Detachment. And the last of these reports which is cited by the Trial Chamber was dated on the 19th of July, 1995, that's two days before members of the El Mujahed Detachment captured the prisoners of war at issue in this case. Then, as we see in the judgement, three days later, on the 22nd of July, another bulletin specifically directed to Rasim Delic provided information that the prisoners were being held by the El Mujahed Detachment and that "so far, they do not allow access." And General Delic did not follow-up on this information, that's from trial judgement 553, and the abuse of the prisoners of war continued until the 24th of August. Why would General Delic countenance the El Mujahed Detachment within his army, knowing their history of criminal behaviour? Because, as we've explained earlier in our submissions, the El Mujahed Detachment was effective in combat. As the judgement shows, it was a specialised assault unit assigned with spear-heading attacks and breaking through enemy lines, the most dangerous assignments in the field. The El Mujahed Detachment was described as "the primary leader" in the July operation that resulted in the capture of the 12 POW at issue in this case. Now, I said "12" there, I said "11" earlier and I'll explain that difference in a second. This tolerance of the El Mujahed Detachment's criminal behaviour is reflected in the 5 July 1995 military security report that Mr. Schneider referred to earlier. I'm just going to go into that in a little bit more detail. As you recall, that report was regarding threats to "slaughter" all the Croats and Chetniks who were in the 1st Battalion of the ABiH 328th Brigade, and this is what that report indicated: "The security body of the 1st Battalion of the 328th Mountain Brigade held separate interviews with permanent top command members and the non-Muslim members and tried to console them, telling them that they were prepared to do everything requested by members of the above-mentioned unit," and of course that's the El Mujahed Detachment, "in order to execute the planned assignments, i.e., occupy Paljenik and Vozuca." And that's from Exhibit 938 and cited in the judgement at paragraph 434. What this illustrates, Your Honours, is the choice of military expediency over any other consideration. Rasim Delic chose expediency, that is, the capture of Paljenik and Vozuca, over his responsibility to enforce international humanitarian law. And as the judgement indicates, in September the El Mujahed Detachment, having never been punished for their crimes against the prisoners of war in July and August, captured a hill called Paljenik, and that's at trial judgement 398. The Chamber found that the apparent impunity with which members of the El Mujahed acted through mid-July 1995, just before the capture of the prisoners, "was also likely to have an encouraging effect on the perpetrators and the El Mujahed Detachment at large," and that's from paragraph 512 of the judgement. Delic's failure to punish the perpetrators of the July crimes showed the members of the El Mujahed Detachment that they could commit even more serious crimes than those recounted by the Chamber in paragraph 501. And again that's the paragraph that lists the bulletins in which Rasim Delic was informed of the criminal behaviour of the El Mujahed Detachment. The murders of at least 53 Serb prisoners in the Kamenica camp by the EMD members in September only serves to illustrate the gravity of Rasim Delic's failure to punish the crimes of the El Mujahed Detachment soldiers in July and August. As the Prosecution has explained in its brief, General Delic's failure to control the EMD before the 21st of July, 1995, was inherently grave, given the enormous powers he exercised as both the highest military commander in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and as a member of the BiH Presidency, which was, as the Chamber described it, "the Supreme Command of the armed forces." And that's at trial judgement 94. The highest military commander in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina has great power, and with this power came great responsibility. Delic had the duty to ensure that international humanitarian law was followed. This principle underpans -- underpins the very idea of command responsibility, Your Honours. As the ICRC commentary to Article 7 [sic] of Additional Protocol I notes: "Everything depends on the commanders," who "more than anyone else can prevent breaches by creating the appropriate frame of mind, ensuring the rational use of the means of combat, and by maintaining discipline." As the commentary says, the commander's failure in his duty to enforce international humanitarian law is "the paramount breach, which encompasses all others." What the Geneva Conventions stand for is that the international community has a fundamental interest to ensure that superior responsibility remains an effective tool in enforcing international humanitarian law. Delic's three-year sentence fails to protect this interest. Delic's failure to prevent and punish the crimes of the El Mujahed Detachment is itself inadequately punished. The three-year sentence additionally fails in the other goal of sentencing at the ICTY, and that is of deterrence. And this is from Trial Chamber judgement, paragraph 559. Not only did Delic fail to prevent and punish members of the EMD for their criminal acts, he personally thanked them for their service and awarded some members of the unit the army's highest award for combat, the Golden Lily. That's at trial judgement 198, and specifically Exhibit 828. His inadequate sentence effectively sanctioned General Delic's decision to ignore his obligations to enforce international humanitarian law and to continue to use the El Mujahed Detachment in battle. The three-year sentence will fail to deter future military commanders from making this same choice, and the three-year sentence diminishes the power of command responsibility as a tool for enforcing international humanitarian law and protecting vulnerable people like the 11 prisoners of war who were ill treated in the Kamenica camp in 1995. Now, that goes to General Delic's -- the gravity of his failure. The three-year sentence also fails to properly reflect the gravity of the crimes committed by the El Mujahed Detachment against the prisoners as the second part of the two-part analysis. As I mentioned, for 35 days the El Mujahed Detachment abused, humiliated, and terrorised 11 of the prisoners. The 12th, Gojko Vujicic, was shot and beheaded the morning after he and the other prisoners arrived in the Kamenica camp. The survivors describe an atmosphere of constant physical and mental abuse that began in the village of Livade on the 21st of July and continued in the Kamenica camp until the 24th of August. One of the survivors, a doctor, a medical doctor, Dr. Branko Sikanic, described how the men were bound by their hands and feet to a stick, forcing their faces to their knees. In his statement he said: "I had a lot of problems with this stick and the terrible position I was tied." And that's from Exhibit 927, cited in footnote 660 of the judgement. In Livade, two of the prisoners were shown the freshly severed heads of two Serb soldiers, identified later as Predrag Knezevic and Momir Mitrovic, who had been murdered by EMD members as an act of terrorisation. The conditions did not improve for the prisoners after they were transferred to the EMD camp in Kamenica. Dr. Sikanic described how the prisoners were restrained once they arrived at that camp. "We were put laying on our stomachs, hands were tied behind our backs, and also our legs were tied. There was some kind of terrible pain caused to my legs, but I am not able to tell what caused that pain. I had a feeling that somebody was slightly cutting off my feet slowly with some object which was moving." And again, this is from his statement which is cited by the Trial Chamber at paragraphs 257 and 258. As I mentioned, Gojko Vujicic was shot and beheaded on the first day at the camp. This had an impact on the others who survived. One of the prisoners of war, Triv icevic, described what he saw. "And one of the Mujahedin who were in the tent at prayer came out of the tent, took an automatic rifle that was right next to the entrance, he cocked it on his way. And then walking, he stopped next to Gojko's head and Gojko could see him coming up, and he just turned his head towards me, to his left. "And then going along, he stood next to Gojko's head and coolly fired a shot at Gojko's right temple and then went back to the tent. And I just looked at Gojko and I could see his little finger still twitching as if he were alive. The Mujahedin went to the tent, then he took a sword. He came back to Gojko and in several strokes he severed Gojko's head. He tried to place this head on the chest, but since the body was tilting backwards, the head wouldn't stay there. He tried it several times, and when that didn't work, he placed the head on the stomach. Then it rolled off ... he put it back on the stomach, and then it stayed there." This is from transcript 3639 to 3640, also cited by the Chamber in paragraph 260. And in the next paragraph, the judgement recalls that the men were made to kiss the severed head. During their stay the men were subjected to regular beatings, electric shocks, and weren't given enough water throughout their imprisonment in the Kamenica camp, and this is from the judgement at 273. This had lasting impact on the victims. As Dr. Sikanic explained: "The serious lack of water caused the dehydration and weight loss, 13 to 15 kilogrammes. As I lost so much weight, my right kidney moved to a lower position than normally. Because of that, I still occasionally have severe pain in the right kidney. As a result of stress and lack of food, I developed an ulcer in the lower intestine," and that is from his statement which is cited in paragraph 268 and 271 of the judgement. Delic's three-year sentence fails to reflect the gravity of the series of crimes, not single crime but series of crimes that were inflicted against these 11 men over a period of 35 days. As the Appeals Chamber has held, superior responsibility is not inherently less grave than responsibility as a perpetrator of the crime. That's at Celebici appeal judgement, paragraph 735. And as Judge Shahabuddeen declared in the Oric appeal judgement: "The punishment for the commander's crime of failing to control his subordinates should be measured by the punishment of his subordinates for the actual crimes committed by them." And that's at Judge Shahabuddeen's declaration, paragraph 22. So Delic is given a three-year sentence. Now, as an example, a conviction for a single instance of cruel treatment under the relevant articles of the SFRY Criminal Code would have resulted in "a minimum sentence of five years' imprisonment," with the most severe penalty being that of death. And that's cited in the judgement. Given the number of victims in this case, 11 -- well, 12, because Gojko Vujicic was also mistreated during his time when he was still alive, and the length of the ongoing abuse inflicted on these men, the appropriate sentence for Delic's perpetrator subordinates would be well in excess of five years. Delic's own sentence of just three years is manifestly inadequate. To conclude, this three-year sentence fails to take into account the critical role that Rasim Delic played in creating the El Mujahed Detachment and in tolerating the behaviour of its members leading up to the July 1995 crimes. He rewarded them when he should have punished them. He deployed them when he should have held them back. The Chamber's three-year sentence was taken from the wrong shelf. It fails to serve as any kind of retribution for these offences. It has no deterrent value to dissuade future commanders from choosing, as General Delic did in this case, military expediency over an obligation to enforce international humanitarian law. The Appeals Chamber should revise this sentence and impose a more appropriate sentence of seven years' imprisonment. And unless there are any questions, that concludes my remarks today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Judges have no questions. I shall now give the floor to the Defence. Mrs. Vidovic, I believe, you are going to be taking the floor and you have 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, again. Your Honours, the Prosecution's submissions contained both in the appeals and those presented today have no foundation in the case law of the Tribunal and have been fully negated through the majority's thorough and argumented analysis. The Prosecutor's plea actually represents an unfounded request for a more severe punishment. As the Prosecution claims in its appeal, the majority has correctly cited all the relevant factors that have to be taken into consideration when sentencing. Namely, according to the Tribunal's case law there are two basic goals of punishment in war crime case. They have both found their reflection in the sentence pronounced. These are retribution and deterrence or, that is to say, the prevention of future crimes. The principle of retribution requires a just and appropriate sentence which is commensurate with the gravity of the act of the accused himself. Deterrence, according to the majority, has two forms: An individual and a general one. However, as the majority has correctly warned in paragraph 559 of the judgement, the principle of deterrence must not be accorded undue prominence in the overall assessment of the sentences to be imposed on persons convicted by the International Tribunal. This position, Your Honours, has been taken by Appeals Chambers in the Kordic and Cerkez cases, paragraph 1078; Celebici, paragraph 801; Tadic, paragraph 48; and Aleksovski, paragraph 185. The majority has correctly evaluated the factors that have to be taken into consideration when sentencing pursuant to Article 24 of the Statute and Rule 101 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Therefore, the Prosecution's appeal is completely unfounded and should be dismissed by the Appeals Chamber. The majority has correctly stated that the gravity of a fact is the crucial factor when determining the sentence. The sentence must reflect the inherent gravity of the act committed by the convicted person, bearing in mind the specific circumstances of the case and the form and the degree of participation of the person convicted in the crime, paragraph 561 of the judgement. This is in compliance with the first goal of retribution. As on all criminal cases, the most important factor in the cases that deal with command responsibility are the acts committed by the accused and the circumstances under which the act was committed. Although the crimes committed by subordinates must definitely be taken into the consideration, the Court must not lose sight of the fact that the convicted person is punished for their own failures and not the offences of their subordinates. This is stated in paragraph 101 in the Krnojelac case, which reads: "It cannot be overemphasised that where superior responsibility is concerned, an accused is not charged with the crimes of his subordinates but with his failure to carry out his duty as a superior to exercise control." The Prosecution ignores the nature of command responsibility and the importance of the acts committed by the accused when it says that the findings by the majority that deal with the nature of the crimes committed by Delic's subordinates illustrate the mismatch between the gravity of the underlying crimes and the three-year sentence imposed. This is paragraph 9 of the Prosecution's appeal. The Prosecution has described in detail the "appalling brutality" of the crimes committed by Delic's subordinates without explaining in what way the gravity of each such described situation should contribute to the sentencing, given that it has been established that Delic did not had actual knowledge about the crimes. Nowhere in the Tribunal's case law is command responsibility defined as strict liability. Therefore, when considering the responsibility of the accused and the appropriateness of the sentence, the conduct of the subordinates must not be afforded too much importance. I again refer us to the case law of this Tribunal, case Celebici, paragraph 239, where it is specifically said that command responsibility is not strict liability; the judgement in Halilovic case, paragraphs 42 to 54, confirmed by the Trial Chamber's judgement; and Hadzihasanovic case, paragraph 66 to 75. The majority, when delivering this sentence, was fully aware of all the details relating to the subordinates' crimes and afforded them appropriate weight in the process of sentences which can be seen in paragraph 564 of the judgement. Contrary to the Prosecution's claims, the possible sentence for his subordinates cannot affect the decision on Delic's punishment because Delic was not convicted of direct involvement in the crimes, but rather, for the failure to prevent and punish his subordinate for the crimes committed. Although the Prosecution correctly states that command responsibility is not per se less serious than the responsibility of perpetrators themselves, it does not follow from this that the superior automatically must be given either the same or even more severe punishment than the one delivered on his subordinates. Command responsibility is another form of a criminal offence, and therefore the punishment must be different, having in mind the nature of the failure of the superior. This is decided by the Trial Chamber in the Halilovic case, paragraphs 42 to 52; and re-affirmed in the Halilovic case, paragraph 39 of the appeals judgement. The Prosecutor mentioned today the case law of the domestic courts and the SFRY Criminal Code. He erroneously invokes the practice of certain legal systems with regard to sentences, because these systems have a completely different concept of command responsibility than the one applied by this Tribunal. In any of the systems mentioned by the Prosecution - and he mentioned a lot today - the severity of the sentence is a very important factor when deciding the punishment for the superior; and the superior himself is therefore considered an accomplice or aider and abetter in the crime. The Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal has specifically stated that criminal responsibility is a separate criminal offence and that those who are convicted on this basis shall not be considered as accomplices, and therefore, their punishment cannot be equal to the punishment imposed on the subordinates. I refer here to the Halilovic judgement of the Trial Chamber, paragraph 42 to 54; confirmed in the Hadzihasanovic case, trial judgement paragraph 66 to 75; and the appeal judgement in the Celebici case, paragraph 239. So the case law of the -- of the courts of the former Yugoslavia in this particular case is of lesser importance. Delic has been convicted for the failure to prevent and punish his subordinates and not for his direct involvement in the crimes. The Prosecution is also in error when taking into account the case law of these courts by overlooking what has been said in paragraph 558 of the judgement. The majority concluded that -- or rather, although the majority stated that jurisprudence must be one of the factors taken into consideration when determining the sentence, in its further analysis it concluded that the SFRY Criminal Code does not contain the form of liability that corresponds to Article 7(3) of the Statute, and that the Tribunal's case law regarding the punishment is relevant for this particular case, paragraph 593 of the judgement. However, as the Prosecutor stated, according to the SFRY Criminal Code the minimum sentence - as quoted in paragraph 593 of the judgement - was five years of imprisonment. However, the sentence pronounced in this case against Rasim Delic is completely adequate and appropriate in view of the fact that he was convicted on the principle of command responsibility and he didn't have actual knowledge about the crimes committed. Therefore, instead of the acts and possible punishment for the perpetrators, the most important factor when sentencing must be the conduct of the accused himself. Since the doctrine on command responsibility theoretically can be applied to a wide spectrum of dereliction or breach of duty which may vary in terms of nature and gravity, so can the sentence to a great extent vary in different cases. There are three basic factors relevant in determining the scope within which a superior can be deemed responsible for the crimes committed by his subordinates and which sentence would be appropriate under the given circumstances. These factors are the gravity of his dereliction of duty, the seriousness of the consequences of such dereliction, and the scope within one might say that his failure to act contributed to the commission of crime, which is failure to act and prevent, or for not imposing punishment on his subordinates. The gravity of the dereliction of duty will be measured by comparing the measures that the accused was legally bound to undertake and had material capability of adopting and, eventually, the conduct adopted by himself in given circumstances. It is important to underline that the superior had some responsibility and relevant authority. One cannot take that as a basis for a presumption that he had a comprehensive responsibility. We also have to bear in mind that according to the international law, a high-ranking officer is neither expected nor requested to personally see to the implementation of measures aimed at preventing or punishing crimes committed by lower-ranking personnel. Please bear in mind the fact that we are talking here about the commander of the Main Staff of the ABiH army, who under him within the chain of command had corps commands, division commands and their commanders, brigade commands and their commanders, battalion commands and their commanders, and the detachment that we are discussing here. So at that level, this detachment only one of the thousand units that existed within that chain. The question which measure or measures a superior must adopt within a given context primarily hinges on the material capabilities that the superior had and the circumstances that prevailed at the time. That was the conclusion of the Trial Chamber in the Strugar case, paragraph 378. Therefore, the Tribunal must have carried out a very specific check of the situation in which the commander was and the means that he had at his disposal during the indictment period, taking into account all the relevant facts of the case. This is in compliance with international law, which clearly imposes that the gravity of failure of the accused as one of the main factors for sentences cannot be established without taking into account all the circumstances in which this failure was committed. This was underlined by the Chamber itself in paragraph 558 of the judgement, and it was also ruled in the Toyoda case, page 5001. Speaking about Delic's failure, the Prosecution claims that a three-year sentence affects the effectiveness of responsibility as an instrument of the implementation of international humanitarian law, having in mind the circumstances of the case. However, the Prosecution did not cite any circumstance that would justify more severe punishment in order -- which would be the way in which the international law would treat the responsibility of a commander. On the contrary, there is a series of circumstances under which Delic was acting which justify the position of the Trial Chamber. The facts clearly show that the circumstances in which Rasim Delic acted from the time he assumed the position of the commander of the Main Staff of the RBiH all the way to the Dayton Accords considerably restricted his capability to undertake any measures against the EMD. On the other hand, the evidence clearly shows that Delic had undertaken all the measures that were available to him under the circumstances. One of the most important circumstances that the Chamber must take into consideration when considering the guilt of Rasim Delic and the appropriate sentence is the fact that his capability of taking any measures against the EMD was even more restricted in view of the fact that this unit refused to recognise the authority of the commander of the RBiH. This was particularly obvious from the fact that members of the EMD did not allow access to representatives of the RBiH to their camps, paragraphs 407 and 410 of the judgement; that RBiH itself had very limited data about the identity of certain members of the EMD, paragraph 373; and as my colleague put it, they didn't know the origin of the countries from which they came; and that this unit persistently refused to accept the system of subordination within RBiH, as testified by Imamovic on the 10th of October, 2007, transcript 4045 to 4046; Sljuka, 24th of October, 2007, transcript 4301-4369; Hajderhodzic, 8th of October, 2007, transcript T-3784 to 3785; Edin Husic, 23rd of October, 2007, transcript 4446 to 4447; Awad, 2nd -- 9th of February, 2008, transcript 172 to 173; and Alija, 16th of October, 2007, transcript 4156. These were all Prosecution witnesses. All the above-stated circumstances are extremely relevant when assessing the individual responsibility of the accused and determining the sentence. It is a relevant fact that Rasim Delic, in spite of the problems cited, has undertaken decisive, albeit often unsuccessful, steps towards establishing a system of command and control in general as well as some -- undertaking some specific measures in order to try and put the EMD under control. Already in June 1993 Delic ordered the 3rd Corps to disarm, disband and expel the Mujahedin, Exhibit 163; then Exhibit 661; then Exhibit 963. In October 1993, he initiated the action Trebevic 1 against two units of the RBiH that were outside of control, as was established by one -- in paragraph 136 of the judgement. Afterwards, he initiated some other actions like Trebevic 2, 3, and 4, respectively, in order to remove obstacles in the functioning of the system of command and control within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as stated in paragraph 137 of the judgement. On the 9th of December, 1993, Delic ordered a clamp-down on the illegal activity of the units of guerilla Mujahedin and El Mujahedin, as stated in paragraph 449 of the judgement. Finally, the operative action Vranduk that you saw, or rather, whose plan you saw, that was the last exhibit that was displayed to you by my colleague, had as its objective investigating the activities of EMD and constituted yet another attempt by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to place El Mujahedin under control. All of these actions indicate that Delic was a responsible commander who tried to establish a system of command and control within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to resolve the problem of the Mujahedin; however, due to a variety of factors that we discussed in greater detail in subground 2D, paragraph 250 through 258 of our appeal, that was not established. The decision of the majority that the Prosecutor calls a twin failure in his appeal is actually a perfectly appropriate judgement in view of the context in which Delic operated. Many difficulties that he encountered on a daily basis no doubt affected his actual ability to prevent and punish. Therefore, Your Honours, the assertion of the Prosecutor that the sentence is inappropriate is far from reality. The majority states in several places in the judgement that Rasim Delic failed to prevent and punish his subordinates, paragraph 564 of the judgement; and on the basis of this it can be concluded that the majority had in mind this twin failure when deciding on sentencing. And therefore, the Prosecution assertion is totally unfounded. The Prosecutor fully neglected certain circumstances, and that was repeated today by the Prosecution to a certain extent, that Delic did not act in accordance with international humanitarian law and that he decided in favour of expediency instead of obligations imposed on him by international humanitarian law.
