Specifically, the Prosecutor says that Delic closed his eyes before violations of international humanitarian law by the EMD and continued to use this unit in operations because that suited his military purposes. This statement is contrary to the findings of the majority. First of all, the majority established that Delic never had any actual knowledge about any crimes, but only had reason to know that the members of the El Mujahedin are preparing to commit a crime of cruel treatment in the camps of Livade and Kamenica in July and August 1995, as stated in paragraph 542 of the judgement. So, for someone who did not have actual knowledge of violations of international humanitarian law, one cannot say that he closed his eyes, as it were, before such violations. Your Honours, you have truly heard some horrifying descriptions. However, none of these descriptions or none of this knowledge ever reached General Delic. And the majority never found any such thing. Secondly, the Prosecution's argument is contrary to the findings of the majority, namely, that Delic worked on resolving the problems related to EMD and that he was involved in training his subordinates on principles of international humanitarian law. And I'm now referring to paragraph 544 of the judgement. Specifically, the majority decided that Delic took measures in order to promote knowledge of and the application of international humanitarian law within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that he instructed commands of the corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to treat enemy combatants who were taken prisoner in accordance with Geneva Conventions and allow the representatives of the ICRC to have access to detention premises, paragraph 544 of the judgement. The Prosecution assertions that Delic decided in favour of military expediency, neglecting obligations imposed on him by international humanitarian law, are totally unfounded. What is also unfounded thereby is what was stated today by the Prosecutor, that the three-year sentence effectively sanctioned Delic's decision to ignore his responsibilities under international humanitarian law and to continue to use the EMD in battle, and that such a sentence has a diminished value as a deterrent. It is not only unjustified, Your Honours, it is also offensive in relation to the Trial Chamber. It does not encourage in any way other commanders to use individuals or units prone to violence in military operations. Also the Prosecution is mistaken when claiming that Delic's decision not to -- or rather, when he mentions Delic's decision not to control the EMD. The majority never found that Delic consciously decided not to control the EMD. The Prosecutor claims that Delic neglected to notice that the El Mujahedin had committed crimes and that he even awarded this unit and thanked it for their services. That is a distortion of facts and findings of the Trial Chamber. In the paragraphs of the judgement, paragraphs 198 and 455, the Trial Chamber found that the recognition given to the EMD was actually there by way of impetus to foreigners to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that promotions of the members of the EMD were a result of the decisions of the Presidency of the RBiH, not decisions of Rasim Delic. Your Honours, that was also referred to in paragraph 455 of the judgement. The Prosecutor completely ignores this context when claiming that the fact that Delic thanked the unit for the assistance they rendered during the course of the war should be taken as an indication for his disregard of international humanitarian law. The findings of the Trial Chamber, paragraph 456 of the judgement, no doubt indicate that Delic's statement was in accordance with the decision of the Presidency and that it was given under pressure that was brought to bear by the international community which, after the signing of the Dayton Accords, asked that all foreigners leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what Witness Loncaric testified on the 10th of April, 2008; Halim Husic as well, on the 12th of March, 2008; also Awad, a Prosecution witness. In such a situation, the representatives of military and political structures had to act highly diplomatically towards foreigners so that they would make sure that they actually left the country. The Prosecutor's assertion that Delic actually deserves a graver sentence because of the fact that his breach of duty to enforce international humanitarian law is especially grave since he was the most senior military commander, that was stated in the appeal and repeated today, is based on an erroneous interpretation of jurisdiction related to command responsibility. Rank or a high position in the hierarchy cannot at the same time be grounds for conviction according to the doctrine of responsibility of the superior and also an aggravating factor in sentencing. Such a procedure would result in taking his position as relevant into account twice, as relevant for sentencing. This was stated in the judgement of the Trial Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case, page 614, footnote 4877; then in the appeal judgement in the Celebici case, paragraph 745, footnote 1261. The fact that the accused held a high position and that he had certain authority can make criminal conduct graver only if the accused person had abused this authority or used it with a view to achieving his own or someone else's criminal acts, and only in situations when the accused person was not found guilty on the basis of command responsibility. Krstic Trial Chamber, paragraph 709; then the appeals judgement in Celebici, paragraph 736; the appeals judgement in Aleksovski, paragraph 183; the sentencing judgement in Sikirica, paragraph 172; the sentencing judgment in Babic, paragraphs 54 through 62; and the sentencing judgement in the Simic case, paragraph 67. Your Honours, the Prosecutor did not prove in any way that Rasim Delic had abused his office or position in any way. The Prosecutor says that Delic was supposed to be given a higher sentence and quotes the appeal judgement in the Strugar case to support that assertion; however, as my colleague already stated, there is an important distinction between these two cases. As opposed to Strugar, Strugar was -- as opposed to Delic, Strugar was found guilty on the basis of Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) of the Statute. The Appeals Chamber in Celebici made a clear distinction between these two forms of responsibility when speaking of sentencing; namely, proof of active participation by a superior in the criminal acts of subordinates adds to the gravity of the superior's failure to prevent or punish those acts and may therefore aggravate the sentence. That is paragraph 736 of the Celebici appeal; and in Aleksovski, it is -- the appeals judgement in Aleksovski, it is paragraph 183. So any kind of comparison between these two cases is inappropriate. Delic was found guilty by the majority of the Trial Chamber only on the basis of cruel treatment and only on the basis of indirect or imputed knowledge of crimes. This last allegation is particularly important in terms of sentencing. The majority itself stated that relevant factors when determining the gravity of a crime of a superior also involved the question whether the superior had actual or imputed knowledge about the crimes committed by the subordinates and the extent to which this was foreseeable. Paragraph 563 of the judgement. And it is important to state that Rasim Delic had imputed and not actual knowledge of these crimes. Paragraph 564 of the judgement. Your Honours, I'm briefly going to deal with what the Prosecutor said today. The Prosecutor said that Rasim Delic had indirect knowledge about criminal behaviour or crimes that had been committed by El Mujahedin previously. That is not true, Your Honours. Even as far as criminal reports are concerned against the killers of Paul Goodall, it does not mean that there are several perpetrators and only some are members of the EMD. On the other hand, the information that was accessible in the bulletins did not have to do with criminal offences at all, but minor offences often committed against civilians. Because of the different traditions involved and the fact that Arab soldiers had different perceptions when compared to those of the Bosnian people. So there is no evidence of previous criminal conduct that Rasim Delic would have to be aware of. The nature of knowledge of a subordinate concerning crimes of -- of a superior concerning crimes committed by subordinates is an important element when looking at the second and third factor relevant and to the extent to which this can be looked into if the subordinates remained unpunished for anything they had committed. I do apologise for being too fast. The Prosecution says in their appeal, in view of his previous role of high-ranking commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Delic's failure to prevent and punish his subordinates is particularly serious because he stimulated the creation of a climate of impunity in the entire chain of control. Delic was the superior of every soldier in the army structure of Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. More than anyone else, he was responsible for exercising the function of command in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is paragraph 33 of the Prosecutor's appeal. When presenting this assertion, the Prosecutor is ignoring relevant jurisprudence and facts in this case. First of all, as for Strugar and Hadzihasanovic, namely, the failure of a commander to punish a crime can be as a consequence an increased risk from having it repeated, can pertain only to a situation where the superior had actual knowledge about crimes committed. I'm referring to Hadzihasanovic appeal paragraph 30, and then the Strugar appeal judgement paragraph 301. Since Delic had only indirect rather than actual knowledge about an isolated incident, one cannot say that this climate of impunity was created by any failure on his part, especially in view of the fact that he actively worked on acquainting members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with international humanitarian law. Secondly, the findings of the Appeals Chamber in the Celebici case that the Prosecutor refers to in his appeal, that constant failure on the part of a commander to prevent or punish crimes of subordinates can encourage subordinates to commit new crimes, paragraph 739, is not applicable in this case, Your Honours. Actually, as opposed to the accused in the Celebici case, the majority did not conclude that Delic on a continued basis failed to carry out his duties. On the contrary, he was found guilty on the basis of the conclusion that he had reason to know of one isolated incident, as stated in paragraph 551 of the judgement. The Chamber itself in the Celebici case states that constant failure on the part of a commander to prevent and punish must be considered significantly graver than cases of isolated incidences of this kind -- incidents of this kind, paragraph 739. The Prosecution's -- the Prosecutor's statement that Delic was the superior commander of every soldier within the military structure of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that more than anyone else he was responsible for command in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is paragraph 33, is contrary to facts and the findings of the Trial Chamber. From the evidence it is clear that the command structure of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is based on singleness of command. So although Delic was the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he did not command all soldiers within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. E 419 clearly states who the persons were to whom Delic was a direct commander, including the commanders of the corps, and so on and so forth, Your Honours. Finally, the Prosecutor ignored many mitigating factors that the majority took into consideration in sentencing. First of all, Delic voluntarily surrendered to the Tribunal immediately after the indictment was issued, as stated in paragraph 573 of the judgement. Secondly, there is an abundance of evidence about his good character; he did not have a criminal record; he was an advocate of implementing international humanitarian law within the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; he was instrumental in the initiation of Operation Trebevic I and subsequent actions to crack-down on unruly units, and he was involved in peace negotiations, as stated in paragraphs 582 through 584 of the judgement. Finally, the majority took into consideration the circumstances that prevailed in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the difficulties that Delic faced because of resistance by persons from his own milieu in certain political groups, paragraphs 588 and 589 of the judgement. The fact that the Prosecutor ignored these mitigating circumstances when asking for a new sentence of seven years clearly states that his request is inappropriate. Your Honours, on the basis of what I've stated so far, it is clear that the majority did take into account all significant factors when asking for an appropriate judgement for Rasim Delic. The three-year sentence reflects the gravity of Delic's failure, all the circumstances in which the failure took place, as well as many mitigating circumstances. The Prosecutor did not present a single valid reason showing why this sentence is inappropriate. The Prosecutor's arguments are contrary to evidence and the findings of the majority and they are based on a misinterpretation, as I've already said, of relevant jurisprudence, and therefore the Prosecution's claims should be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Pocar has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: As just a question to be clear about what your position is, because perhaps I didn't get it correctly through the interpretation. Is that correct that your point is that command responsibility is a separate crime consisting of the failure to prevent or punish separate, distinct, from the crime committed by the subordinate? Is that correct what I heard?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If it is so, is that your point that command responsibility is not responsibility for the crime committed by the subordinate, but is a different kind of responsibility that is not linked necessarily to the crime committed? I heard you saying that it depends on the gravity of omission of the duty measured in light of the measures that the commander should have taken. So is that correct, your point is a quite different offence which has nothing to do or very little to do with the crime committed by the subordinate? In other terms, it is not a mode of responsibility for the crime committed by the responsibility, but is a completely different offence. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Our position and the position of the majority of Trial Chambers in this International Tribunal is that this is a separate crime, that this is a distinct crime. In other words, a commander is responsible for his own failure to either prevent or punish, but not for the crimes committed by his subordinates as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. In such a case, am I correct that in your view, the gravity of the failure to prevent or punish is not dependent on the gravity of the crime committed by the subordinate? That has to be measured differently?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, yes, Your Honours. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Meron has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If I may follow on the penetrating questions asked by my distinguished colleague, Judge Pocar. You are in fact saying in answering him that there is no nexus between the gravity of the sentence to be imposed, say, on Mr. Delic and the conduct of his, let's assume, subordinates without going into the question of effective command now. Would that also be your position if Mr. Delic would have known what were the crimes committed and how grave they were; or are you resting your argument, or your answers to Judge Pocar on the fact that he was not familiar with what was happening in the Mujahedin compound?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, actually no. General Delic should be convicted on the basis of his own credibility, that is to say -- actually, yes, I apologise. I made a mistake. General Delic should be tried and convicted on the basis of his own failure and the gravity thereof, that is to say, his failure to prevent and pressure. Certainly, the gravity of the crimes committed should be taken into account, but in no way should it be accorded too much importance, because otherwise one can always assume that every commander should get life imprisonment for any serious crimes committed by his subordinates. Therefore, we have to judge his own failure and his own liability. And, Your Honours, allow me to answer the second part of your question. Of course it is extremely important in this situation to know whether he was convicted due to the existence of actual knowledge or indirect knowledge. If he didn't have any actual knowledge about the specific circumstances, then definitely it is a different kind of failure as opposed to the situation in which he had actual knowledge. Had he had actual knowledge, his failure would have been more serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are no other questions. Therefore, Mr. Prosecutor, you have 20 minutes for your reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The most important point to take away from the Prosecution's submissions, Your Honour, and in response to what the -- in reply to what the Defence has said today, the Prosecution's argument here is that the Chamber failed to properly assess the gravity of crimes and also the gravity of Rasim Delic's breach. The circumstances as a whole on the facts of this case, as applied to Rasim Delic, this is -- this three-year sentence is manifestly inadequate. I heard a lot in response that imputed knowledge should be treated as something different than actual knowledge, and that was repeated throughout the Defence submission today and throughout their brief, and this is an important point to address, I think. The reason that Rasim Delic did not have actual notice of these crimes is because of a failure to inquire further when he had alarming information about prisoners being held by this particular unit out of a thousand, after he had received information that this particular unit out of a thousand, as the Defence says, had a propensity to commit violent criminal acts. To say that he should be given a lower sentence because he only had imputed knowledge versus actual knowledge, only rewards his failure to inquire further when he got this information. There's nothing in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal that suggests imputed knowledge should be treated anything differently than actual knowledge, and that is not a step that the Appeals Chamber should take in this case either. A few other points. The Defence said that there should not be undue prominence given to deterrence. Now, that's obviously in the jurisprudence. The Prosecution agrees with that proposition, but that doesn't in any way have any effect on their arguments in this case. Retribution -- or deterrence should not be given undue prominence, perhaps, but it should be given some prominence. The Prosecution's argument in this case is that the three-year sentence for these crimes under these circumstances, considering Rasim Delic's knowledge of the criminal behaviour of the EMD shows that the deterrence has actually no prominence, and that is where the Trial Chamber erred. Now, there's also some debate about -- in response to some questions about whether the criminal acts of the accused or of the perpetrators is transferred to the commander under 7(3). Now, there is some dispute about whether 7(3) is actually a crime of failing to prevent or punish, or whether the commander convicted under 7(3) is actually convicted of the crimes themselves. But for this case, Your Honour, that's not a discussion that needs to be delved into that deeply because even on the facts and the law as the Chamber has described them or has recounted in this case, Rasim Delic's failure in this case on these facts shows that the three-year sentence is inadequate. Now, even if you agree that the crimes of the perpetrator are not imputed to the commander, the case law is still very clear that there must be some correlation between the likely crime of the subordinate and the crime that the commander would receive. Now, in this case I did go into some detail about the gravity of the crimes themselves, and it's important to remember this is not a low-level cruel treatment case, Your Honours. This was cruel treatment inflicted on first 12 and then 11 prisoners of war over a period of 35 days, on a daily, constant basis. It's important to bear that in mind and to consider that the perpetrators in this case would certainly, under virtually any standard, have been given a sentence of more than three years. Now, whether that should be -- whether Rasim Delic's sentence should be equal to that of what the perpetrators received, that is not what the Prosecution is arguing necessarily. The Prosecution's argument is that there should be some correlation, and that for crimes that are this grave, considering especially the fact that Rasim Delic was on notice that the EMD was holding vulnerable prisoners and that the EMD had a propensity for criminal violence, the three-year sentence is manifestly inadequate. As to the Defence argument that the Prosecution fails to take into account the difficult circumstances under which Rasim Delic was functioning, the Prosecution's contention here is that this three-year sentence is manifestly inadequate, even considering - this is what we said in our reply brief as well - even considering the mitigating circumstances that the Chamber found. Even taking that into account, this is still a manifestly inadequate sentence. Another major theme, of course, was that Rasim Delic chose military expediency over international humanitarian law, his obligation to enforce that. That was on page 100 of the transcript today. The evidence as a whole in this case, Your Honours, shows that Rasim Delic knew based on the notice that he'd received, as recounted in paragraph 501 of the judgement, and of course I'd invite Your Honours to take a close look at paragraph 501 which does show exactly what kind of notice he received. The Chamber found that the notice that was recounted in paragraph 501 showed that he knew starting in 1994, and even perhaps as early as 1993, that the El Mujahed Detachment had a propensity for violence, had a propensity for criminality. Rasim Delic continued to employ the El Mujahed Detachment notwithstanding that. That shows, Your Honours, that he did choose military expediency over his obligation to enforce international humanitarian law, and that culminated in the report that he received or the report that was directed to him specifically on the 21st of July, the bulletin, which showed that -- the 22nd of July, which showed that the El Mujahed Detachment had members -- or had prisoners of war in its possession and was refusing to allow access. He had an obligation at that point to do something or at least to inquire further, and it's his failure to do so that resulted in the cruel treatment of these men until August 24th, for 35 days. Just a couple other points, Your Honours. As for the Defence argument that the rewards were only given to the El Mujahed Detachment as an impetus for them to leave, that is a mis-characterisation of the findings of the Chamber. Your Honour, if you look at paragraph 455, it shows that a number of El Mujahed Detachment members were promoted by a decision of the Presidency, of which General Delic was a member even in June 1995, at various moments before the final ceremony where Rasim Delic attended and thanked the El Mujahed Detachment for their service. They were being promoted even during their service as an effective fighting force for the army. So to say that they were only given awards and promotions because of an impetus to leave, the evidence doesn't show that. And finally, the Defence suggests perhaps that the Prosecution argues that we want his position of authority to be counted twice and that it's only an abuse of a position of authority that can be counted as an aggravating circumstance. Now, the Prosecution agrees with that proposition. It says that's pretty clear in the jurisprudence that only an abuse of authority can be considered an aggravating circumstance; but that's not what the Prosecution's argument is in this case. The Prosecution doesn't suggest that his high position should be counted twice, but rather that it should be properly assessed the first time in assessing the gravity of his breach. As the Prosecution has said in its brief, Delic in a position -- more than anyone else had a position or was in a position to intercede in July 1995 when he got information or when that information was directed to him that these men were being held and that access was not being provided to them. One additional point. As to the culture of impunity, this feeds into the Defence argument that imputed knowledge should be treated differently than actual knowledge. The Chamber found in paragraph 512 that the failure to punish the El Mujahed Detachment members for the series of crimes going back to 1994 had to have an encouraging effect on them and did create a culture of impunity. That's straight from the Chamber's finding at paragraph 512. Unless there are any further questions, if I could just consult with my colleagues for just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you finished, Prosecutor? We don't have any questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Absent any further questions, we're now going to turn to Mr. Delic and ask him whether he has anything to say to the Appeals Chamber. In the affirmative, he may proceed but not for more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that will be more than enough. First of all, it is my duty to thank you for giving me the floor to say a few words. I don't want to go into legal evidence and the legal situation as it is because, on the one hand, it is the task of the Prosecutor to prove what they wish to prove; we on the Defence side want to prove what the truth is; and you have your own duty as the Appeals Chamber. It is my duty to say that I trusted this Tribunal as an army commander at the time when it was being established. Because of the situation in my country, I believed that this Tribunal was needed in order to have my own country advance, that is to say, to have reconciliation and progress in my country. Through my own efforts, I supported the work of this Tribunal up until the end of the war, until 1995, and afterwards as one of the commanders of the joint army of the Federation. So irrespective of the punishment meted out by the Trial Chamber, I still trust this Tribunal to decide on the basis of law and legal arguments. I have no doubt in that regard. I would like to thank you for these fair proceedings and I am grateful for the fact that these proceedings took place in a fair way without any incidents involved. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Delic. Let me now thank the Legal Officers, the representative of the Registry who helped us hold this hearing, the court reporters for their very invaluable help, as well as the interpreters that -- who made it possible for us to communicate. We are now going to deliberate. You will be informed of the date for the appeal judgement in due time. Thank you very much. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.01 p.m.
